Dune Director Admits He’s ‘Deeply Disappointed’ by Showdown With Avengers: Doomsday

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (459 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Polygon)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, denis Villeneuve isn't thrilled about having to share a release date with Marvel's next Avengers movie.
  • "The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic.
  • Recent findings suggest that villeneuve stated he had hoped the third movie would finally enjoy a more straightforward theatrical release, without a pandemic or industry shutdown complicating its prospects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, denis Villeneuve isn't thrilled about having to share a release date with Marvel's next Avengers movie. The Dune: Part Three director has admitted he's "deeply disappointed" after Disney scheduled Avengers: Doomsday for the same December release date as his upcoming sci-fi sequel. In an interview with Time, Villeneuve discussed the unusual box-office showdown between the two highly anticipated films, both of which are scheduled to open Dec. 18.

"The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us," Villeneuve told Time, pointing to the challenges surrounding the first two installments. Dune: Part Two was originally expected to arrive in the fall before being pushed to the end of winter because of the Hollywood strikes.

Recent findings suggest that villeneuve stated he had hoped the third movie would finally enjoy a more straightforward theatrical release, without a pandemic or industry shutdown complicating its prospects. Instead, Marvel's biggest franchise is now going head-to-head with his film.

"So I was deeply disappointed," he noted. "But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema.".

Recent findings suggest that villeneuve acknowledged that Dune doesn't have the same commercial muscle as the Marvel Cinematic Universe, describing Avengers as a "T. rex" and his franchise as a "sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower." Villeneuve's first two Dune films made $411 million and $715 million at the worldwide box office, while Marvel's Avengers movies have consistently grossed in the billions. "I'm no fool. Those movies are a mammoth," he said, adding that he hopes Dune: Part Three will survive the box-office competition.

Still, the filmmaker isn't necessarily viewing the simultaneous releases as a straightforward rivalry. He suggested the two movies could combine to create one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time. "Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not," Villeneuve told Time. "But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.".

Dune: Part Three will adapt elements of Frank Herbert's Dune Messiah, picking up years after the events of Dune: Part Two. Timothée Chalamet returns as Paul Atreides, alongside Zendaya, Florence Pugh, and other familiar faces. Villeneuve has also described the movie as a significant departure from the source material, explaining that the adaptation required substantial creative choices.

Avengers: Doomsday marks the next major ensemble installment in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, with Robert Downey Jr. returning to the franchise in a fresh role as Doctor Doom. Both films are presently scheduled to hit theaters on Dec. 18, setting up a potentially massive "Dunesday" weekend for movie theaters.

Magic: The Gathering Designer Reveals 2026’s 11 Best Fresh Commanders

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Polygon)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With 2026 delivering a packed release schedule for Magic: The Gathering exploring classic planes and several Universes Beyond crossovers, Commander players have had plenty of exciting fresh legends to build around.
  • Recent findings suggest that when Polygon spoke with Magic: The Gathering Principal Designer Gavin Verhey about the year's lineup at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026, he walked through each major release to highlight what he considers some of 2026’s most powerful Commanders.
  • Industry observers note that we all love abilities that trigger when something enters the battlefield, don’t we?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With 2026 delivering a packed release schedule for Magic: The Gathering exploring classic planes and several Universes Beyond crossovers, Commander players have had plenty of exciting fresh legends to build around. From returning to familiar fantasy worlds in sets like Lorwyn Eclipsed and Secrets of Strixhaven to epic crossovers like Marvel Super Heroes, The Hobbit, and Star Trek, the year brought an unprecedented wave of Commanders for casual and competitive tables alike.

Recent findings suggest that when Polygon spoke with Magic: The Gathering Principal Designer Gavin Verhey about the year's lineup at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026, he walked through each major release to highlight what he considers some of 2026’s most powerful Commanders. Rather than focus strictly on raw power ceilings, Verhey pointed toward the legends that spark creative brewing, surprising table politics, and memorable gameplay moments across every 2026 release. Here's a look at this year's 11 best Commanders in the order they were released.

Industry observers note that we all love abilities that trigger when something enters the battlefield, don’t we? Well, Maralen, Fae Ascendant takes that to the tenth degree by bridging two of Lorwyn's most recognizable kindred types into a nimble value engine that’s entirely too fun to abuse. Whenever Maralen or another elf or faerie enters under your control, she exiles the top two cards of a target opponent's library, letting you cast one exiled spell each turn for free if its mana value is equal to or less than your Elf and Faerie count.

Verhey noted that "Maralen turned out awesome" and pointed out that "a lot of people have built that one." He has pitched team-up legends for years, and seeing her succeed makes him eager to explore more dual-type pairings like Rin and Seri or Olag and Miau.

Rather than singling out a single hero from the Turtle Power! Commander precon, the standout attraction here is the modular roster built around the “Partner — Character select” mechanic. Inspired by classic arcade beat-'em-ups, the keyword lets you mix and match eligible legends, like Leonardo, the Balance alongside Raphael, the Muscle or Donatello, the Brains, to tailor your Command Zone synergies.

As Verhey explained, "I think the interchangeable Character Select partner mechanic in the Commander deck is pretty awesome there." He added that he loves how these legends "can be interfaced and spliced together," noting that players have gravitated toward the pairings because they combine partner flexibility with punchy abilities. Pairing Leonardo, the Balance with Raphael, the Muscle gives you a prime example, since putting a +1/+1 counter across your board on token entry and doubling damage from creatures with counters lets modest boards turn lethal in a single turn.

It has been revealed that at six generic, one black, and one green mana, Witherbloom, the Balancer carries affinity for creatures and extends that exact same cost reduction to every instant and sorcery spell you cast. Flooding the battlefield with tokens or cheap mana producers turns hefty spells like Army of the Damned and Shamanic Revelation into effortless plays. Once you pair that discount with token doublers like Chatterfang, Squirrel General, even splashy finishers like Exsanguinate or Torment of Hailfire become trivial to fire off for lethal.

It has been revealed that secrets of Strixhaven is loaded with what Verhey described as "banger commanders," and the designer admitted he could easily name around ten standout legends from the set. Even in that crowded lineup, Witherbloom, the Balancer rises to the top as a blast to build around, especially alongside spell-copying payoffs like Professor Onyx and graveyard recursion staples like Eternal Witness.

It has been revealed that this double-faced mythic rare gives Azorius builds strong flexibility at flash speed. On his front face, King T'Challa draws you a card whenever any player draws their second card each turn, and you can pay six mana total to transform him into Black Panther, Hope Enduring. The opposite side of the card yields a double-striking threat with flash that prevents damage dealt to him and draws cards on combat hits, making him especially lethal with equipment staples like Sword of Feast and Famine or unblockable auras like Steel of the Godhead.

Verhey pointed to T'Challa and Black Panther as a standout among cards that fit traditional color expectations while still "tearing up tables." Surrounding him with symmetric draw engines like Howling Mine or wheel effects ensures his front side triggers across every turn cycle before he flips to close out the game.

Industry observers note that at a single white mana, Nick Fury, Agent of S.H.I.E.L.D. looks modest on paper until you read his Power-up ability. Since Power-up reduces its activation cost by his mana cost when he enters that turn, Fury adds two +1/+1 counters to himself while digging seven cards deep to drop a Hero, Equipment, or Vehicle straight onto the battlefield. It’s solid flavor for a 2/1 creature, and has a lot of potential if you know the right way to abuse it.

Verhey described Fury as "really unassuming" yet potent, noting that "Nick Fury, the one-mana white commander, has been really strong." He also shared that he was running all five free spells once Fury hits the board for a single mana.

It has been revealed that the Hobbit brought Middle-earth's more whimsical side to Commander with standout legends like Bilbo Baggins and Thorin Oakenshield, yet Smaug the Magnificent is an absolute beast among them. Built to snowball fast, the 4/3 legendary dragon with flying and haste, and even nets you a treasure token at the start of your upkeep. Worst of all, however, is Smaug’s main ability, which deals damage to any creature equal to the amount of treasures you have whenever he attacks.

It has been revealed that verhey noted that "Smaug Treasure decks look pretty cool" and called him a "really powerful Commander," which is saying something. For just four mana, the creature not only stacks treasures for you every single turn, but also deals a little extra damage where needed, best used to chip away at a player’s life total or creature-filled battlefield. Even worse is that Smaug can swing right when he gets onto the battlefield thanks to haste, so if you already have a slew of treasures by the late game, he’s dealing some serious damage that can be made even more devastating with red staples like Furnace of Rath and Fiery Emancipation.

Just like Smaug, Radagast of Rhosgobel also hails from The Hobbit set, bringing instant-speed tempo to mono-green decks. His static ability discounts the first creature spell you cast each turn by two generic mana and lets you cast it as though it had flash, essentially saving you mana for interaction before deploying threats on an opponent's turn.

Recent findings suggest that the Hobbit offers strong options across the board, according to Verhey, who said, "I like the Radagast decks I've been seeing that discount your spells when you play one a turn." That opens the door for surprise plays like flashing in Kogla, the Titan Ape for instant removal or dropping discounted threats like Ghalta, Stampede Tyrant right before your untap step. While I’m not running him as a commander, I have a Radagast in my Thalia and the Gitrog Monster deck, which is all around sacking creatures and land.

As a color-shifted twist from the Reality Fracture Commander decks, Dack Fayden, Helping Hand, puts a fun spin on a well-known Magic character. Upon entering, Dack reveals cards from the top of your library until you hit creature cards equal to the number of your opponents. He then puts those creatures onto the battlefield permanently goaded and hands one to each opponent, stirring up chaotic table politics with a hint of group hug thrown in.

Recent findings suggest that calling the white Dack Fayden "kind of a funky one,” Verhey suggested he might be the answer for raw power in the set. Players who pair his trigger with blink staples like Ephemerate or symmetrical payoffs like Homeward Path and Trove of Temptation can quickly turn messy handouts into a one-sided advantage.

According to recent reports, liliana the Faultless flips familiar Magic lore in the Echoverse-themed Reality Fracture, becoming a white-aligned version of the character that gains you a life whenever another creature or planeswalker you control enters. You can also pay one mana and discard a card to grant another creature or planeswalker you control hexproof until the end of turn, giving mono-white decks a steady form of protection.

It has been revealed that while Verhey also shouted out the set's white Leonin legends and his own black Abzan precon designs, Liliana fits neatly alongside those experiments. Her discard-to-protect clause pairs cleanly with planeswalker or token commanders like Elspeth, Sun's Champion and Mondrak, Glory Dominus that want extra shield equity.

True to his trickster reputation, Q, Stacking the Deck shuffles your library on entry and exiles cards from the top until he hits a nonland card, letting you repeatedly copy that exiled spell by discarding cards from your hand on your turn. Various brewers have already pushed this to remarkable extremes with 98-land decks built to guarantee hitting a specific combo piece.

Verhey admitted he still loves Q and wants "to believe that Q has something pretty wacky," framing him not necessarily as the strongest card in the set, but as one "on my radar" that plenty of players are already building around. Slotting Glaring Fleshraker into a 98-land Q deck, for example, reveals just how wild things can get, since exiling lands from your hand to chain copies of Fleshraker floods the board with Eldrazi Spawn tokens that pay for the next copy and ping the entire table out of the game in a single turn.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a lot of TV to watch this weekend, whether you’re tuning in to highlights that are already airing or looking for your next binge.
  • The Rings of Power has been releasing new episodes on Tuesdays, with the finale airing on Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that when it comes to fresh offerings, there’s plenty of exciting stuff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Happy Thanksgiving! There’s a lot of TV to watch this weekend, whether you’re tuning in to highlights that are already airing or looking for your next binge.

The Rings of Power has been releasing new episodes on Tuesdays, with the finale airing on Nov. 24 (be sure to check out our Sauron explainer). We’re also covering new episodes of Yellowjackets, which air on Fridays (The series premiere revealed one of its biggest mysteries).

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to fresh offerings, there’s plenty of exciting stuff. Blade Runner: 2099 premiered this Wednesday, set in a new world where Replicants have replaced humans as the world’s dominant force. If you’re looking for something juicy and bingeable and very awkward for family viewing, The Hunting Wives just premiered its sophomore season, depicting more murders in Texas.

There are plenty of international TV reveals this week, including Always on Call and Fool Night, with some anime and reality TV shows newly available to stream. Happy watching!

According to recent reports, set 50 years after Blade Runner: 2049, the series completely shuffles things around. After exploring the dynamics with humans and replicants in two beloved films, the latest TV show finds humans as the underclass. The story follows Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human on the run pretending to be a Blade Runner in order to secure a future for herself and her brother.

While Blade Runner 2049 was a direct sequel that continued the story of Harrison Ford’s Rick Deckard, Blade Runner 2099 creator and showrunner Silka Luisa focuses more on exploring the franchise’s themes than advancing its plot. Fifty years after the events of the 2017 film, the Replicants once used as slave labor out in space have led an uprising and now rule Los Angeles. Rather than searching for rogue Replicants, Blade Runners brutally enforce order amongst the humans unlucky enough to be trapped on the barely habitable planet. Desperate human fugitive Cora (Hunter Schafer) is offered a chance at a fresh start if she can impersonate a Replicant to steal something from the police evidence room. When Cora discovers a rogue Blade Runner already took her prize, she has to team up with his former partner Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) to find it.

Recent findings suggest that the Netflix overnight phenomenon The Hunting Wives is back for a second season, building on the first season and novel. This time around, the show is telling an original story, continuing the tale that was first laid out by the book. The newly introduced season finds Sophie (Brittany Snow) at a turning point: she killed Margo’s (Malin Akerman) brother, leaving her with another secret to hide amid their complicated relationship.​​​​​​​.

If you're into Norwegian dramas,​​​​​​​ Always on Call is now on Netflix. The Norwegian series follows a surgeon who has just started working at an overwhelmed emergency room that serves as a last resort.​​​​​​​ Each episode explores new cases and workplace medical drama that continues to satisfy viewers of all sorts.

Sources indicate that netflix’s latest dystopian anime is set in a world without sunlight, where humanity relies on an optional medical intervention called transfloration. Volunteers are paid handsomely to have a flower implanted in them; it blooms two years later and provides oxygen for others.​​​​​​​ The series follows an impoverished boy who agrees to the procedure, gaining an ability that allows him to hear the voices of Spiriflora. He soon finds himself drawn into a complex conspiracy.

Based on the manga by Kasumi Yasuda and directed by Atsuyuki Yukawa, Fool Night is a surprisingly intimate story set against an enormous environmental catastrophe. Rather than throwing viewers into an expansive science fiction mystery, Yukawa takes his time introducing its main characters and how their lives become intertwined by circumstances neither could have anticipated. It's a more methodical introduction than some might expect, offering plenty of room to establish the people at the center of a world literally steeped in darkness and comforted only by the discarded remains of the volunteers transformed into grotesque flora.

In a recent development, netflix’s new three-part documentary series explores the death of police officer John O’Keefe and the case against his girlfriend, Karen Read, who was believed to be the prime suspect. She faced two murder trials.​​​​​​​.

According to recent reports, netflix’s latest reality TV competition follows Salish Matter, a YouTube star who invites seven of her closest friends to a snow-covered getaway for holiday-themed party games. But, since this is 2026 and things can't be that simple, there's an impostor in the group, whose mission is to sabotage all challenges and steal the gifts without anyone else noticing it.

Netflix’s staple holiday cooking series is back with two latest episodes.​​​​​​​ The Great British Baking Show: Holidays is a spin-off of the beloved cooking show, with previous competitors returning for a season themed around Christmas and New Year’s Day.​​​​​​​.

Blue Exorcist follows a teen raised by an exorcist priest who discovers he's the son of Satan and a human woman. His journey of vengeance against his father begins when Satan tries to claim him as a vessel, with the priest and caretaker sacrificing himself to protect him. The series’ third season is now available on Netflix.

Any shōnen that leverages religious mythology and symbolism to flesh out its world-building is already off to a great start, and Blue Exorcist makes good use of this premise. Two mirror dimensions exist: Assiah, the material world for humans, and Gehenna, the demonic realm ruled by Satan. The demons often breach through the earthly realm via human possession, which is why we have Exorcists, who secretly work for the Vatican and take down these threats. Our protagonist is Rin Okamura (and to an extent, his twin Yukio), who learn that they’re sons of Satan after witnessing their human father’s death.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the most powerful CPU on the market, AMD's Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, is down to its lowest price ever of $759 this Black Friday.
  • In a recent development, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 has an MSRP of $900, but it released at $1,000 before settling back down to $900.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 is AMD's first dual-CCD CPU with 3D V-Cache.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the most powerful CPU on the market, AMD's Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, is down to its lowest price ever of $759 this Black Friday. By the numbers, it's the best CPU for gaming, and the fastest in multithreaded workloads. It's also the first processor AMD has ever created that uses its 3D V-Cache across both CCDs.

In a recent development, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 has an MSRP of $900, but it released at $1,000 before settling back down to $900. Although we've occasionally seen $50 off the CPU here and there, this is the first time we've seen this steep of a discount. The processor is on sale for $799 at most retailers, knocking $100 off its list price. On Amazon, however, an on-page coupon knocks off an additional $40, bringing the price down to $759.

Recent findings suggest that the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 is AMD's first dual-CCD CPU with 3D V-Cache. It sports 16 cores and 192 MB of L3 cache, and it can boost up to 5.6 GHz.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D features 128MB of L3 cache, which enables it to claim the title of the fastest gaming chip on the market. It features 16 Zen 5 cores and 32 threads of computing power, reaching a peak clock speed of 5.7 GHz.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D, which features the stacked cache on a single CCD, is also on sale for $115 off, bringing its list price of $699 down to $583.55. For most people, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D is the better buy. Outside of a few niche applications, it performs identically to the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 across games and productivity workloads.

You can see that reflected in the charts above, which we gathered during our Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 review. Regardless of which processor you go with, you're getting top-shelf gaming performance. The Ryzen 7 9850X3D is a touch faster, but realistically, this is identical gaming performance in practice.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 has a small 4% advantage over the Ryzen 9 9950X3D in multithreaded workloads, and the two perform identically in single-threaded workloads, falling short of Intel's latest Core Ultra 7 270K Plus.

In a recent development, we recommend the Ryzen 9 9950X3D for most people, but if you want the best of the best, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 at $759 is an excellent deal. Make sure to pair it with a quality CPU cooler (ideally an AIO), as well as a midrange to high-end B850E or X870 motherboard.

It’s Officially the End of an Era for HBO’s The Last of Us

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (395 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Polygon)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it's officially the end of the road for The Last of Us at HBO.
  • Recent findings suggest that casey Bloys, chairman and CEO of HBO and Max content, shared several updates on upcoming projects with Deadline in September, following a successful night at the Emmys for the organization.
  • Industry observers note that mazin is the co-creator and showrunner of the series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it's officially the end of the road for The Last of Us at HBO. While the upcoming third season was already set to conclude the show's adaptation of the second game in Naughty Dog's acclaimed PlayStation series, there was some hope it could continue on after. Those hopes have now been squashed by HBO's boss.

Recent findings suggest that casey Bloys, chairman and CEO of HBO and Max content, shared several updates on upcoming projects with Deadline in September, following a successful night at the Emmys for the organization. That included The Last of Us, with Bloys saying that, "Craig [Mazin] has planned it as the final season.".

Industry observers note that mazin is the co-creator and showrunner of the series. After The Last of Us, he's moving on to create a Dungeons & Dragons show, a sequel to Baldur's Gate 3, for HBO.

After adapting the first game in the first season of the show, HBO split The Last of Us Part 2 across two seasons to reflect the game's dual protagonists. Season 2 tells the story of Ellie's (Bella Ramsey) quest for revenge following the death of Joel (Pedro Pascal) and her hunt for Abby (Kaitlyn Dever). Season 3 will flip the perspective, retelling the same period of time as season 2 from Abby's point of view. This will also introduce the character of Lev, played by Michelle Mao.

Neil Druckmann, co-creator of the game series, co-created the HBO show alongside Mazin. Druckmann served as a showrunner and writer for the first two seasons but stepped away from work on season 3. Recently he has continued to distance himself and Naughty Dog from the show, especially after the response to the second season was less than stellar. In a recent interview with The Washington Post, he affirmed that Naughty Dog had no creative role in the final season before teasing that he still has looks for the future of the franchise.

As for when season 3 of the show will actually be released, Bloys reiterated that it is scheduled for 2027. He didn't give further details on a specific date or window beyond that. Don't worry though, as Sony is at the moment working on a God of War series for Prime Video starring Dave Bautista. The hunger for more game adaptations will be sated.

According to recent reports, it’s Fangsgiving here at Polygon, our Thanksgiving celebration of stories about fanged creatures of all types and especially vampires. I didn't want to be left out, but, to be honest, I always thought vampires were kind of dumb. They're a horror movie staple, but they’re rarely all that scary. There’s usually a romantic element to their stories that I also find tiresome. Perhaps I’ve just never seen the right vampire movies, but overall I find vampires to be pretty lame.

The only vampire character I ever really had any affection for is Grandpa Munster from the 1964 black-and-white sitcom The Munsters.

The Munsters debuted in 1964 and lasted for just two seasons, but in that time they produced a whopping 70 episodes. The show is about a family of monsters living a normal life in the suburbs and freaking out nearly everyone they encounter. The head of the family is Herman Munster (Fred Gwynne), who is Frankenstein’s monster. He is married to a vampire named Lily (Yvonne De Carlo), and they have​​​​​​​ a werewolf son named Eddie (Butch Patrick). Also living with them is their entirely normal, non-monster niece, Marilyn (Beverley Owen/Pat Priest). And best of all is Grandpa Munster, a several-hundred-year-old vampire​​​​​​​ played by Al Lewis.

According to recent reports, while Lily, Eddie and Marilyn were amusing characters in their own right, the best episodes and moments of the show focus on Herman and Grandpa — especially when the two are at odds, which is often. Herman is a dim-witted, affable, optimistic monster, but he can get a bit petulant and baby-like when he doesn’t get his way. Grandpa, meanwhile, is a scheming inventor who often toils away in the family basement, which serves as his laboratory​​​​​​​, which is a frequent source of funny stories on the show. He's very smart, very sarcastic, but also emotional. He’ll quickly become jealous of not being included in something or will overreact to small slights. Also, because he’s hundreds of years old, a recurring gag has Grandpa talking about knowing long-dead historical figures like Genghis Khan and Jack the Ripper.​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, Grandpa is a pretty crappy vampire. A running gag on the show is his trying (and failing) to bite people. He also can go out during the day and casts a reflection without glitch. So, really, he’s a vampire in name only, which might scare off some vampire purists. But if you’re interested in checking out some great Grandpa-centric episodes of The Munsters, here are five of the best.

Sources indicate that another running joke in The Munsters is that Grandpa has been married many, many times — 167, according to one episode — but when a woman from Sioux City, Iowa, claims​​​​​​​ that Grandpa is her lost husband, he’s certain that she isn’t. That is, until Grandpa finds out the woman is incredibly rich. Suddenly, Grandpa is sure this is his wife and decides to move in with her.

Industry observers note that grandpa is feeling lonelier than usual, which prompts him to call the services of a matrimonial agency he finds in the newspaper. Grandpa then turns all of his eccentric charms on a seemingly normal woman​​​​​​​, all of which should scare her off, but they don’t. In time, we find out she’s a black widow scheming to marry Grandpa and then kill him off.

Eddie wants to bring a pet to school for the pet fair, but the family’s pet dragon “Spot” and pet bat “Igor” refuse to go. So Grandpa turns himself into a bat and pretends to be Igor and lets Eddie take him to school​​​​​​​. Unfortunately, Eddie and a friend with a pet squirrel decide to trade pets for the weekend. If that weren’t bad enough, Eddie’s friend’s dad is an astronaut who aims to shoot the bat into space.

According to recent reports, after Herman wrecks the Munster Koach in a race, Grandpa builds the Drag-u-la, a race car built off a coffin body. This episode is especially good because it focuses squarely on the hilarious Grandpa/Herman relationship, complete with conflict and some camaraderie​​​​​​​, as the two end up scheming to win together.

Recent findings suggest that another great Grandpa/Herman episode features the two making a normal trip to the bank​​​​​​​, where they are mistaken for a pair of robbers wearing Halloween masks. They are swiftly given all the money in the vault and then must figure out how to return it without looking like they are crooks returning to the scene of the crime.

#800. 8 Classic PlayStation Games That Are Barely Playable Today

📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1527 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Polygon ↗ Open Full Page

8 Classic PlayStation Games That Are Barely Playable Today

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Polygon)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve ever watched someone play an old PlayStation game and wondered why their character keeps spinning around in circles, congratulations, you’ve already met tank controls.
  • The dealbreaker: Lining up one jump means turning in place, backing up, taking a run-up, and holding a grab button in midair.
  • Reminder: Tomb Raider is a platformer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever watched someone play an old PlayStation game and wondered why their character keeps spinning around in circles, congratulations, you’ve already met tank controls. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s your quick introduction: With tank controls, pressing up moves your character forward in whatever direction they’re facing, and pressing left or right only rotates them, so with the stick alone, you can’t sidestep or turn on a dime. That’s manageable in a hallway. It’s much less so when you’re sneaking past a guard, lining up a shot, or timing a leap across a pit, which is why the same scheme caused trouble in just about every genre during the PS1 era. These eight classic games are the hardest to go back to, whether the culprit is tank controls or something else entirely.

The dealbreaker: Lining up one jump means turning in place, backing up, taking a run-up, and holding a grab button in midair. Every single time.

Reminder: Tomb Raider is a platformer. You’re jumping roughly every 15 seconds, and most of those jumps demand precision measured in single pixels. The tank controls were supposed to help players thread that needle, but they also meant holding down a series of buttons in a specific order at perfectly timed moments, every few seconds, over the course of a whole game. Here’s what a “big” jump looked like in practice: Walk to the edge, hop back once, run forward, jump at the last second, and hold the grab button while in the air. All while counting the number of blocks you’re jumping around and using specific button combinations for standing, running, and walking jumps. If you guess wrong, game over.

The good news is that Aspyr’s 2024 remaster lets you switch to modern controls, with the camera on the right stick, or keep the classic scheme if you’re feeling brave. A full remake, Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, will be released in February 2027. In the meantime, take comfort in the one polite thing Lara does: she’ll never walk off an edge, though she’ll happily run directly off one.

The dealbreaker: A fear meter instead of a health bar, and a game that punishes you for running out of ammo.

In a shooter, running out of ammo is a special kind of stressful. Here, you’ll follow three mercenaries as they chase a supernatural conspiracy through Hong Kong in 2050. What starts as a job to retrieve a Triad boss’s daughter turns into a descent into a surreal version of hell, with Triads, zombies, and demons along your journey. Get spotted or take a hit, and your character’s fear will climb. Helpfully, so will the danger you’re dodging. Fear Effect uses tank controls, which trap you more often than they allow you to run. A 2025 re-release from Limited Run Games made the tank controls optional, and added widescreen, rewind, and save states. It’s maybe the nicest thing anyone has done for tank controls: Made them optional.

The dealbreaker: A zombie in the next room, and a camera angle that can’t see it.

Recent findings suggest that not being able to see a threat lurking around the corner is possibly the point; it does heighten the terror in this game significantly. Resident Evil helped define the survival horror genre, and the fixed camera angles are part of that. You steer Jill or Chris, two members of the Raccoon City police’s elite S.T.A.R.S. unit who get trapped in a mansion infested with zombies, with tank controls — which means “forward” always means forward for the character, regardless of the camera angle you’re working in. That consistency helps when the view cuts every time you cross a doorway, but combat suffers, since you’re lining up shots at things you often can’t see. Your stiff, complex movements don’t help either.

In a recent development, if you want the original experience, the Director’s Cut, which adds analog stick support, is available on PS Plus Premium. If you want the best way to play the first game, though, the 2002 remake (and its 2015 HD remaster) features a rebuilt mansion with new graphics, lighting, and revised layouts.

The dealbreaker: You can look in first person, but you can’t shoot in it.

This is the kind of thing that sounds like a minor detail until you’re trying to sneak past a guard. Snake, a legendary soldier pulled out of retirement to infiltrate a remote Alaskan nuclear weapons facility, can switch to a first-person view to scout. But when you need to aim, you’re back in the top-down camera, often at an angle that doesn’t show you the person you’re trying to shoot. This is a stealth game where the stealth mechanic is extremely unforgiving. The sequels get a bit better, fortunately. If you’re interested in giving the original a go, it’s playable in Master Collection Vol. 1 on PC, PS5, Switch, and Xbox Series X. Even though it’s unwieldy, at least it’s short: you can finish it in a handful of hours.

The dealbreaker: “DANGER!” prompts that take your controls away at the worst possible moment.

Clearly, this is a recipe for disaster. The setup here is delightfully silly: You’ve got a secret research island, a missing scientist, and a government project that has gone very wrong. (Spoilers: There are dinosaurs involved.) Imagine Resident Evil, but with dinosaurs, and you’ll get the right idea. You play as Regina, a special ops agent on a mission to rescue a scientist named Dr. Kirk. Tragically for the doctor, you move with tank controls under a camera that follows you instead of staying fixed.

In a recent development, capcom tried to mitigate this with a quick-turn button, but Dino Crisis takes your controls away exactly when you’d want them most. At scripted points of the game, that “DANGER!” prompt flashes on screen, during which surviving means button mashing, not steering. Everything you’ve carefully practiced, your turning, aiming, and running skills instantly become irrelevant, and if your reactions aren’t fast enough, you’re punished.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

The dealbreaker: Armored enemies, and a very slow manual aim.

Recent findings suggest that A shooter lives or dies depending on how fast you can land headshots. Syphon Filter is Sony’s stealth-and-shooting spy thriller, starring secret agent Gabe Logan. Gabe’s job is to stop a deadly virus, and the game wants you to play it like a fast-paced spy movie. If only that were possible! It’s not quite tank controls, but Syphon Filter is very unresponsive and awkward to play. You see this most when you try to shoot. The game does give you lock-on aiming, but that doesn’t help when your enemy is wearing body armor…so you need to switch to a slower first-person aim, anyway, to go for the head. So the skill the game cares about the most, landing a headshot on an armored guard, is the one it makes you do slowest. While enemies shoot you from off-screen. Have fun with that!

The dealbreaker: A role-playing sequel that swapped turn-based battles for real-time shooting, with controls so stiff that learning them is the hardest boss.

This is a strange reinvention for a series that started as a turn-based RPG. Aya Brea, a former NYPD officer, now works for an FBI unit that hunts creatures created by mutated cells. In the sequel, she fights in real time, with tank-style controls. You explore pre-rendered backgrounds, lock on to enemies, and dodge as you investigate a monster outbreak that starts in a Los Angeles shopping tower and leads to a deserted town in Nevada. The toughest part of Parasite Eve 2 isn’t a boss or a random encounter but mastering what one contemporary reviewer called “the stiff and stubborn playcontrol,” though it gets easier after an hour or two. That’s the good news. The bad news is that you still have to spend that hour or two developing that muscle memory.

The dealbreaker: It’s very difficult to find on modern consoles, and the original code got lost.

In a recent development, now this is a different kind of unplayable. For the original Silent Hill, access to the actual game is your main enemy, not necessarily the odd controls or unforgiving gameplay. Here, you’re playing as a man searching a fog-covered town for his missing daughter. The 1999 game itself is out of reach on modern consoles: its publisher has acknowledged that the source code was lost, so for a very long time it couldn’t be officially ported or remastered. (A fan decompilation project just finished reconstructing the original code, which could open the door to unofficial ports someday.) Your options for playing this today are an original PS1 disc or, for now, the PS3 store.

Sources indicate that if you want the series on a modern console in the meantime, there’s the Silent Hill 2 remake, Silent Hill f from 2025, and Townfall. For now, the best way to play the first Silent Hill is a PlayStation, a disc, and a lot — a lot — of patience for dealing with fog.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anything can be the star of a Far Side comic.
  • Here are the seven funniest Far Side comics that star food, some of which feature food that has even gained sentience for the sake of a perfect joke.
  • It has been revealed that I love this comic strip because it is just unabashedly silly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anything can be the star of a Far Side comic. While most of them featured stupid humans or talking animals as their main characters, the surrealist streak in cartoonist Gary Larson sometimes gave life to inanimate objects as well. For example, there’s a strip where a jogger tells a living pair of scissors that they can no longer run together. And if scissors can be alive in The Far Side comics, just about anything can, including food.

Here are the seven funniest Far Side comics that star food, some of which feature food that has even gained sentience for the sake of a perfect joke.

It has been revealed that I love this comic strip because it is just unabashedly silly. Not only are sandwiches alive in this one-panel reality, but they have such a complex social structure that they even have their own organized crime. The sandwich mafia is so cruel that it punishes its victims by hurling them into a pit of fourth-graders. If I were the sandwich, I’d be especially worried about the fourth-grader in the green stripey shirt. He looks vicious.

Sources indicate that yet another food item that has turned to a life of crime. Here, Larson interprets potato salad going bad in the silliest way possible​​​​​​​.

It has been revealed that this is a twist on that classic gag where, with two people in a life boat, one begins to imagine the other as food. This one features​​​​​​​ a man and a cow in a lifeboat​​​​​​​, so the man naturally imagines steak while looking at the cow​​​​​​​. As for the cow, well, he dreams of the man as a pile of man-shaped grass.

I love how adorable-looking these man-eating bears are as they stumble upon a group of campers in sleeping bags and exclaim “Sandwiches!” Personally, I think of sleeping bags as more burrito-like or even more like pita bread than sandwiches, but perhaps these bears aren’t terribly educated about the ways other cultures eat.

It has been revealed that one of the reasons why The Far Side endures more than 30 years after Gary Larson concluded his strip is that he never spoke down to his audience. Sure, he had some dumb jokes sometimes, but they were never dumbed down for our sake; they were just dumb​​​​​​​ for the sake of being dumb — like a sandwich mafia. Larson could pull off the lowbrow and the highbrow, often in the very same comic, as this one illustrates​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that at a glance, it doesn’t even seem like there’s a joke here, despite the simple caption​​​​​​​: “Soup of the day is ready!” This is one of those comic strips by Larson that demands that you go looking for the punchline. Larson seems to trust that the audience will find the joke (or maybe he doesn’t care if some don’t, which I applaud). Eventually, you see that this chef is missing his shoe, meaning he used it to make the soup. So for all that highbrow thinking you had to do to find the punchline, the joke is incredibly lowbrow. It’s the perfect mix.

According to recent reports, larson also got into really dark humor at times. He once drew a comic strip where a snake killed himself by becoming his own noose, which is both silly and incredibly macabre. Yet this food-centric panel is so dark that it borders on creepy. Who is this guy that wants to buy this young employee of the butcher? And who is this butcher that is willing to sell him?

I first read this comic strip when I was a teenager, around the time when I first discovered The Far Side and quickly became obsessed with it. Since then, every time I make a waffle, I cannot help but think of this comic strip. I’ll mix the batter, spray the waffle iron, pour the mix in, close the top, and wait for that little light to go off. Inevitably, as I’m staring at that little light, I’ll murmur, “Slave to the waffle light.” It's one of those pieces of art that just speaks to a real-life truism.

When making waffles, we are all Wendell Zurkowitz.

#791. Stop Building AI Into Your Product. Let Your Customers Bring Their Own.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1442 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Stop Building AI Into Your Product. Let Your Customers Bring Their Own.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1442 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Entrepreneur)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • It has been revealed that over the past two years, almost every software tech giant has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated.
  • Sources indicate that I run a company that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It has been revealed that over the past two years, almost every software tech giant has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated. So we all did. Chat panels appeared in the corner of every dashboard. “Summarize with AI” buttons indicated up next to every text field. Pricing pages grew a fresh line item for AI credits.

Sources indicate that I run a company that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too. But somewhere along the way, I noticed something about our customers that changed how I think about the whole question.

Industry observers note that if you sell to businesses, look at what your customers’ employees have open on their screens. Very often it’s a corporate Claude or ChatGPT subscription, or Microsoft 365 Copilot bundled into the Office licenses the organization was paying for anyway. Someone in IT or finance evaluated it, signed a contract, went through a security review and rolled it out.

In a recent development, that assistant is becoming the company’s “at-home AI.” It’s the one employees are trained on, the one legal has approved, and increasingly, the one that has context about the business: documents, email, meeting notes, internal wikis. Every company will have one eventually. Frankly, most already do.

Now imagine that same company uses eight or 10 business tools, and each of those vendors has bolted on its own AI assistant. Each one has a different interface, different limits and different data policies. None of them know what the others know. The help desk AI has no idea what was discussed in the CRM, and the CRM’s AI can’t see the project tracker.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not a better workplace. It’s AI sprawl, and it’s the opposite of what the customer wants.

It has been revealed that the alternative is simple: Instead of building an assistant into your product, make your product easy for the customer’s existing assistant to use. Let them bring their own agent.

Recent findings suggest that if that phrase sounds familiar, it should. A decade ago, “bring your own device” (BYOD) changed how companies thought about laptops and phones. More recently, “bring your own key” (BYOK) let customers plug their own AI provider’s API key into software instead of paying the vendor for AI usage. Bring your own agent (BYOA) is the next step: The customer doesn’t just bring the key; they bring the whole assistant, with its context, its permissions and its security approvals already in place.

It has been revealed that for the customer, the benefits are obvious. They use a tool they already pay for and already know. Their assistant can combine data from your product with everything else it has access to. Asking “which of our biggest accounts filed support tickets this week, and what did we promise them in the last renewal call?” only works if one assistant can see both the help desk and the meeting notes.

For the vendor, the benefits are less obvious but just as real.

You stay out of the token-reselling business: When you build AI features on top of a model provider, you’re effectively buying compute wholesale and reselling it. Your costs grow with usage, your margins depend on someone else’s pricing changes, and you end up designing credit systems and usage caps instead of building your actual product. With BYOA, the customer’s AI subscription covers the compute. Your product provides the data and the actions.

You stop competing with companies that spend billions on models: No software vendor of normal size is going to build a better general-purpose assistant than the frontier AI labs. Trying to match them feature for feature is a losing race. Being the best tool their assistant can connect to is a race you can actually win.

According to recent reports, it clarifies product decisions: This one surprised me the most. Once you accept that the customer’s assistant will handle the conversation, the question shifts from “What AI features should we build?” to “What can our product do, and how cleanly can we expose it?” That’s a much healthier question. It pushes you to make your core functionality solid, well-structured and well-permissioned, which is good for every user, not just the ones using AI.

It’s a marketing channel, too: This is the least obvious benefit. AI clients now have their own connector directories, and there’s a growing number of independent MCP registries and listing sites. Getting listed puts your product in front of people at the exact moment they’re looking for tools to connect to their assistant. It’s a new distribution channel, it’s still relatively uncrowded, and it costs you nothing beyond the integration you were building anyway.

Industry observers note that this doesn’t mean built-in AI has no place. Some features, such as automatic ticket categorization that runs in the background without anyone asking, make sense to keep inside the product. But the conversational assistant, the one people talk to, increasingly belongs to the customer, not to you.

In a recent development, the practical way to do this today is to implement an MCP server for your product. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that lets AI assistants discover and use tools in external applications. It’s supported by Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot Studio and a growing list of other clients. You describe what your product can do, such as search records, create items or upgrade statuses, and any compatible assistant can use those actions on the user’s behalf, within that user’s existing permissions.

There are two common ways to ship an MCP server, and the choice matters more than it seems.

1. A hosted endpoint over HTTP: Your product exposes an MCP endpoint on its own servers, using the protocol’s streamable HTTP transport. The customer adds a URL to their assistant, signs in, and that’s it. Nothing gets installed. When you add fresh capabilities or fix a bug, every customer gets the update immediately, because there’s only one version: the one you’re running.

2. A local package. You publish a command-line tool or npm package that runs on the user’s machine and talks to your API. This was the common approach early on, and it still works for individual developers.

According to recent reports, I strongly recommend the first option. We started with both at my company, and we’re now phasing out the local package. Each installed copy is a version you can’t upgrade, and customers running old packages kept missing newer features.

Industry observers note that but the bigger reason is security. Large organizations increasingly won’t allow third-party code to run on employee machines, and for good reason. The past couple of years have brought a steady stream of critical-severity vulnerabilities and software supply chain attacks, including compromised packages in the npm ecosystem itself. Asking a security team to approve a package that runs locally with access to company data is a hard sell. Asking them to approve an HTTPS endpoint on a vendor they’ve already vetted is a much easier conversation.

It has been revealed that A hosted endpoint also fits how companies roll out AI. Organization-wide connectors in enterprise AI aims are typically set up once by an administrator and then made available to everyone. Support OAuth sign-in so each employee connects with their own account and permissions, and you’ve removed most of the friction.

It’s tempting to view the customer’s AI assistant as a competitor for attention. If people spend their day in Claude or Copilot, won’t they spend less time in your product?

Industry observers note that maybe. But they were going to use that assistant anyway. The real question is whether it can reach your product when they need it. If it can’t, you’re the tool that gets worked around. If it can, you’re part of how the firm works.

B2B buyers don’t want another AI. They want the one they already have to work with everything else they pay for. Build for that.

Over the past two years, almost every software company has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated. So we all did. Chat panels appeared in the corner of every dashboard. “Summarize with AI” buttons showed up next to every text field. Pricing pages grew a upcoming line item for AI credits.

Industry observers note that I run a firm that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too. But somewhere along the way, I noticed something about our customers that changed how I think about the whole question.

A Bigger Business Isn’t Automatically a Better One. Here’s What to Ask Before Scaling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve spent 13 years building a business. It’s long enough to figure out what works, and definitely long enough to get a lot of things wrong. When we were five people in a 300-square-foot office, our team tripled in size in a year. Our client base and revenue grew just as quickly. At some point, I genuinely started to believe we were the gods of consulting. As it turned out, we were simply very good at running a small tech giant.

Recent findings suggest that that is one of the lovely things about early success. It gives you confidence and the impression that you have figured out the whole business. Now that I’ve had time to reflect, I see that the first lesson of scaling is that success at one stage doesn’t automatically prepare you for the next.

If a team of five can become 10 by working harder and talking more, it’s tempting to assume that 10 can become 50 the same way. But growth is not multiplication. A firm of eight people and a company of 30 are not the same business at different sizes. They are two different organizations that require two different ways of managing.

In its early days, a small organization can get by on instinct, proximity and a good deal of improvisation just because, as a founder, you are involved in nearly everything. You know the clients, notice the work, answer questions and make decisions often before anyone has had time to schedule a meeting about them.

Industry observers note that for me, the hardest part wasn’t letting go of tasks. It was realizing that the quality of my business now depended on decisions I wasn’t making, and sometimes didn’t even know were being made.

This is a transition I didn’t handle perfectly. One of my wrong calls was appointing people to management roles because they were excellent specialists. It seemed reasonable at the time, but expertise in consulting doesn’t automatically equip someone to lead a team or resolve a conflict. The difference becomes significant when the business depends on managers to preserve quality without the founder standing nearby.

I am convinced that a company must become less dependent on its founder at precisely the moment the founder may feel most protective of it. That requires more than delegating tasks. I’d say develop leaders who can exercise judgment, establish standards that don’t live solely in the founder’s memory and distribute authority with enough clarity. Without it, founders often remain the final decision-makers, even after building several layers of management.

Sources indicate that if you recognize your business in this stage of growth, Ichak Adizes’s model of the manufacturer life cycle offers a useful way to understand this transition. The entrepreneurial “Go-Go” stage, with its energy and instinct for opportunity, eventually gives way to “Adolescence,” when informal habits must yield to professional management and clearer authority.

Industry observers note that these growing pains don’t necessarily mean you’re running a bad business. On the contrary, they may simply mean you’ve outgrown the way you used to run it. This model gives founders a way to understand why the habits that helped a young organization move quickly may no longer serve the organization as it grows.

One of the easiest traps to fall into when scaling is that you can become so busy building the firm that you forget who you’re building it for. You can look at your dashboard, see rising revenue and new sign-ups, and think you’re winning. Meanwhile, right under your nose, the quality your loyal clients are getting is quietly tanking.

It’s incredibly easy to lose sight of the customer when your calendar is consumed by recruitment and endless alignments. You end up stuck in back-to-back meetings talking about structure, while your actual clients are dealing with junior staff who don’t fully understand their business yet.

Ask yourself, when was the last time you personally spoke to a client not to sell them something, but to understand whether your organization is still delivering the value they expect?

As a business grows, the cost of complexity grows with it. More employees mean more coordination, more management responsibilities and more opportunities for processes to break down. Before committing to another expansion push, it’s worth looking at the reality of the market.

OECD figures show that among SMEs with 10 to 249 employees, 8% to 14% qualified as employment scalers in 2020, while 12% to 24% qualified as turnover scalers. The OECD also found that scalers were, on average, 20% more productive than other SMEs before their high-growth phase, with that advantage rising to 35% after three years.

What this reinforces for me is that expansion should never be an automatic next step. I try to keep that question front and center; otherwise, you can become so absorbed in perfecting the company’s internal structure that you stop thinking about the actual person using your product.

So before the next growth effort, make sure you do not scale chaos:.

Not every business needs to become bigger. Sometimes scaling creates value. Sometimes it simply creates overhead. More employees do not automatically mean more success. More markets do not automatically mean more opportunities. And higher revenue does not necessarily mean a healthier business.

In specialist consulting, a focused team of 10 can be more profitable and resilient than an organization of 50. In fintech, entering another country may be strategically sound, or it may add cost and complexity without improving the customer proposition.

When we were five people in that small office, I thought learning to make money meant I knew how to build a big business. It took me 13 years to realize that building a bigger firm and building a better company are not the same thing.

I’ve spent 13 years building a business. It’s long enough to figure out what works, and definitely long enough to get a lot of things wrong. 📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As we power toward the holidays, the shopping pressure is officially on.
  • As we power toward the holidays, the shopping pressure is officially on.
  • Amazon buries its best discounts on purpose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As we power toward the holidays, the shopping pressure is officially on. Your natural instinct may be to type what you need into the Amazon search bar, click the first Prime-eligible result, and pay whatever price the algorithm spits out. That’s a huge mistake. Amazon buries its best discounts on purpose. The retail giant operates three distinct clearance portals where you can score open-box electronics, overstocked gifts, and refurbished tech for up to 70% off retail. Before you pay full price for holiday gifts this year, here’s where you actually need to look. Amazon Resale Formerly known as Amazon Warehouse, Amazon Resale is where Amazon sends customer returns. The trick to using Resale is understanding its strict grading system. If you buy an item rated as Used—Like New, it means the product itself is in perfect, untouched condition, but the original shrink wrap is broken or the cardboard box has a minor dent. You get a massive discount simply because the packaging isn’t pretty enough to sit on a retail shelf. If you’re buying tech gear or kitchen appliances where the box just goes straight into the recycling bin anyway, it’s the easiest way to save hundreds. Just stick strictly to the Like New or Very Good tiers. Amazon Outlet Unlike Resale, everything in Amazon Outlet is brand new. This is where Amazon dumps seasonal overstock and excess inventory that’s taking up too much physical space in its fulfillment centers. Finding it is the hard part. It isn’t advertised on the home page. You have to type amazon.com/outlet directly into your browser or dig deep through the Deals and Savings menu on the mobile app. Once you’re in, you’ll find everything from holiday decorations to winter apparel marked down by 50% to 70%. It’s the absolute best spot to hunt for stocking stuffers and white elephant gifts without breaking the bank. Woot Amazon bought Woot back in 2010, but it still operates as a standalone site at woot.com. It’s a dedicated daily deal platform that runs flash sales on electronics, tools, and apparel until the inventory sells out. Just be prepared to act fast, because the best tech deals usually vanish before your morning coffee gets cold. It’s called Amazon Haul, and the gimmick is simple: Every item comes from outside the U.S., which often means cheaper, direct-from-manufacturer pricing. While you lose next-day delivery—items can take up to a couple of weeks to arrive—and the return window drops to just 15 days, every purchase is still backed by Amazon. That makes it a safer way to buy ultra-cheap phone cases, kitchen gadgets, and holiday party supplies without risking a scam.

If you buy an item rated as Used—Like Latest, it means the product itself is in perfect, untouched condition, but the original shrink wrap is broken or the cardboard box has a minor dent.

Sources indicate that you get a massive discount simply because the packaging isn’t pretty enough to sit on a retail shelf. If you’re buying tech gear or kitchen appliances where the box just goes straight into the recycling bin anyway, it’s the easiest way to save hundreds. Just stick strictly to the Like New or Very Good tiers.

Unlike Resale, everything in Amazon Outlet is brand new. This is where Amazon dumps seasonal overstock and excess inventory that’s taking up too much physical space in its fulfillment centers.

Industry observers note that finding it is the hard part. It isn’t advertised on the home page. You have to type amazon.com/outlet directly into your browser or dig deep through the Deals and Savings menu on the mobile app.

#782. Tech Report: Screwed up at work? Here’s how to learn from your mistake without overcorrecting

📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1784 w)

Tech Report: Screwed up at work? Here’s how to learn from your mistake without overcorrecting

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Part of what separates great leaders and employees from merely good ones is the ability to learn effectively from mistakes.
  • Recent findings suggest that part of what separates great leaders and employees from merely good ones is the ability to learn effectively from mistakes.
  • That is, we focus too hard on the most recent failure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Part of what separates great leaders and employees from merely good ones is the ability to learn effectively from mistakes. Often, we talk about learning from mistakes as if most people don’t. But while we can always point to a few people who seem blissfully unchanged by their errors, a more dangerous trend is the continuous attempt to fight the last war—which ultimately leads to ineffective learning. That is, we focus too hard on the most recent failure. Our biggest concern becomes avoiding the mistake or bad outcome that happened last. As a result, we forget the many other lessons we have learned. That tendency to make significant changes based on the most recent mistake can lead our behavior to veer wildly and lead to other mistakes down the line. Here are three things you can do to avoid changing too much as the result of an error. 1. Focus on the smallest fix posible When you make a mistake at work, and particularly when it’s a massive one, it tends to dominate your thinking. The consequences may still be felt across the organization, and you’re embarrassed. You may even imagine that everyone you see is thinking about what you did wrong. Because this recent error is at the forefront of your mind, you are likely to emphasize avoiding that same mistake in the next thing you work on. Unfortunately, when you do that, this error is going to be overrepresented in the planning you do for whatever project you’re working on next. You may become so focused on that problem that you miss other potential difficulties. You may even change routines that have served you well in the past just to avoid the same mistake again. Instead, when you develop an idea about how to correct your mistake, think intentionally about the smallest thing you can change. If you purposefully underemphasize the change you want to make, that will provide a counterweight to the attention you’re paying to that recent mistake. It will help dampen the tendency to overreact. 2. Think about what works If you’re a reasonably conscientious person, you probably don’t make mistakes all the time and, in fact, are probably successful at most of what you do. However, it’s likely you find the errors you do make to be embarrassing and unacceptable. You certainly don’t want to make the same mistake twice. But instituting a correction needs to be done in the context of the many things that you do well. It is certainly vital to do some kind of after-action report to determine what went wrong that led to your mistake. But after you figure out what went wrong, make sure that you also think about what goes right most of the time. Understand how your current way of working leads to good outcomes most of the time. The aim is to ensure that when you make a correction, the changes you make preserve as much of what typically leads to good outcomes as possible and focus just on those things that are most likely to lead to the mistake you made. 3. Track your learning We live in a limited window of the present. That is, it is hard to remember all of the things that you do that have become habits and how those influence the effectiveness of your work. You might be able to remember your work style from a few weeks ago, but the way you did your work last year or the year before that may feel like a mystery. It can be even harder to remember what aspects of work you struggled with. It can be helpful to keep a diary of the way you work, your struggles, and the biggest mistake you can remember from a given time period. Every three months, put a half hour on your calendar to update your journal. Write about the three key projects you’re doing at that moment. Think about the changes you have made to your work routines over the past few months. Write about what aspects of work are going well and which feel like a struggle. When you make a mistake at work, go back over that journal and read about the evolution of your work over time. Reading your journal has several benefits when you’re dealing with a new mistake you have just made. It reminds you of ways you have struggled in the past that are no longer a problem. It may remind you of changes you made in the past that you are no longer keeping up and should return to. It can also give you a sense of the many ways you have improved your workflow over the years. All of these elements can be helpful when correcting a mistake. When you are no longer struggling with things that caused you fits in the past, it helps you to be aware that the habits you developed are largely successful. You may also realize that your current mistake reflects that past changes have fallen by the wayside and need to be reinstated. Recognizing the many ways you have adapted your work over the years can also help you to avoid undoing past changes in the zeal to avoid a current mistake. All of these can help you to right-size the correction you are making now.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that by harnessing potent antibodies that can vanquish diverse viral strains, scientists are closing in on one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine for HIV.
  • Industry observers note that the world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine.
  • Pregnancy causes drastic changes to the brain, but we know little about them because of past worries about the safety of scanning pregnant people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

It has been revealed that by harnessing potent antibodies that can vanquish diverse viral strains, scientists are closing in on one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine for HIV. This year, several research teams described vaccination strategies that triggered the production of these broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) in monkeys, and precursors to bnAbs in people, suggesting that an effective vaccine is possible. But devastating cuts to US funding for HIV research have left some efforts in limbo.

Industry observers note that the world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine. It also has a drug capable of preventing infections: the long-acting injectable drug lenacapavir, which could avert an estimated one-third of new HIV infections in Africa if given to just 5% of adults. Now is the time for funders to ramp up investment, not cut it back, argues a Nature editorial.

Reference: UNAIDS & Gates Foundation report.

Pregnancy causes drastic changes to the brain, but we know little about them because of past worries about the safety of scanning pregnant people. Now, researchers are working to fill that void by collecting scans from first- and second-time mothers and analysing thousands of archived brain scans acquired during routine clinical care. The work, presented last week at the US Society for Neuroscience annual meeting, could help to explain maternal mental-health conditions such as postpartum depression.

In a recent development, ‘General purpose’ artificial-intelligence tools such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude are impressing researchers with their emerging biology skills, including protein design and structure prediction. In some tests, these models have even outperformed those designed specifically for biology tasks and trained on vast troves of protein-sequence data. Some scientists predict that generalist AI tools could eventually catch up with, or surpass, blockbuster models such as AlphaFold. Others suggest these latest abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data, rather than advanced learning.

As I write, the United States army is preparing to detonate around 4.4 tonnes of unstable lead azide, a chemical used to make munitions, at an ammunition plant in Iowa. “It's essentially a lead bomb,” indicates occupational and environmental health researcher Patrick O’Shaughnessy. “Now it's a matter of how much gets ejected out of the bunker.” Academic researchers have banded together to gather independent public data about the plume of toxic lead dust that is expected to spread over the area.

Figure 1 | Position verification. a, To check the location of a party called the prover, two verifiers each send a random bit (a challenge), which are timed to reach the location simultaneously. The prover combines the bits and returns the answer. Because no signal travels faster than light, a prompt reply shows that the prover is at the location. b, However, if two adversaries, one near each verifier, copy a challenge and pass it to each other, they can answer in time even though nobody is at the claimed location. c, In Kavuri and colleagues’ scheme, one verifier generates two entangled photons, keeping one and sending the other to the prover. Both verifiers then transmit classical challenges. The prover uses the challenges to determine how to measure its photon and returns the result, while the first verifier measures the other photon. If the prover’s result arrives in time and the two measurements pass a statistical check (a Bell test), the transmitted photon must have been measured at the claimed location.

Industry observers note that “Banks, power grids and satellite-navigation systems all depend on knowing where a request or a signal comes from, yet claims about location are notoriously easy to fake,” notes physicist Davide Bacco. Now researchers have outlined an experiment in which the position of a distant party is certified using quantum entanglement.

In a, two verifiers send random bits (challenges) timed to reach the claimed location simultaneously. The prover combines them and replies. Because signals cannot travel faster than light, a prompt response verifies the prover’s location. But two adversaries (b) can defeat this test by exchanging the challenges and responding in time. In (c), a verifier also sends one of two entangled photons, which are inexorably linked in a way that can be proven using a statistical check (a Bell test). If the prover’s result arrives inside the time window imposed by the speed of light and the photons pass the Bell test, the prover must be inside the target region. (Nature | 9 min read).

According to recent reports, chemist George Whitesides made landmark contributions to many fields, including patterning surfaces with molecules — a technique that enabled ‘lab on a chip’ diagnostic devices — advances in nanotechnology and more. He prided himself on switching research interests often, telling students, “If somebody else is working on something, don’t work on it.” In traditional chemistry departments, “there’s often a lot of pressure to stay in your lane, and he made it okay not to”, notes polymer scientist Joseph DeSimone. “In fact, he made it exciting not to.” Whitesides has died, aged 87.

Read Whitesides’s guide to writing a scientific paper in a special problem of Advanced Materials that celebrated his 65th birthday.

Some mental disorders seem to take different forms in different places, writes mental-illness researcher Alexander Pereira. “Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears,” he writes — with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, prevalent in China, and psychological symptoms, such as low self-esteem, more common in the West. Pereira argues that our ability to adapt to our social environment might significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental health.

In a recent development, changing location — even just walking through a doorway — can signal to our brains that work is over and it’s time to relax, states cognitive scientist Joan Ongchoco. (BBC Future | 11 min read).

Reference: Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology paper.

The stunning geological formation was buried in the 1886 eruption of Mt Tarawera, but it will never be forgotten.
