#648. Magic: The Gathering’s Most Notorious Vampire Almost Broke Commander

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1419 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Polygon ↗ Open Full Page

Magic: The Gathering’s Most Notorious Vampire Almost Broke Commander

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Polygon)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, most Commanders in Magic: The Gathering have to show up on the battlefield before they can do anything.
  • Sources indicate that nine years after his debut in Commander 2017, Edgar ranks second on EDHREC, with more than 52,000 decks tracked over the past two years.
  • While most people spend Black Friday buying presents for the holidays, we at Polygon celebrate all things vampire and vampire-adjacent with Fangsgiving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, most Commanders in Magic: The Gathering have to show up on the battlefield before they can do anything. But Edgar Markov can make you the most dangerous player at the table while he’s still sitting in the Command Zone. Cast a one-mana vampire on your first turn, and Edgar gives you a second vampire for free. Do it twice on turn two, and you have six creatures before some players have cast their first spell.

Sources indicate that nine years after his debut in Commander 2017, Edgar ranks second on EDHREC, with more than 52,000 decks tracked over the past two years. Given his Eminence ability, which Wizards itself has admitted was a mistake, it's easy to see why.

While most people spend Black Friday buying presents for the holidays, we at Polygon celebrate all things vampire and vampire-adjacent with Fangsgiving. So let’s talk about the guy who sired an entire plane’s worth of vampires and then became one of Magic: The Gathering’s most lethal (and controversial) Commanders.

Magic actually introduced Edgar’s grandson first. Sorin Markov debuted as a mono-black vampire planeswalker in 2009’s Zendikar, where he had unfinished business with the Eldrazi he’d helped imprison thousands of years prior. Two years after that, Innistrad took players to Sorin's home plane. In Wizards of the Coast’s A Planeswalker’s Guide to Innistrad, a description of a hilltop estate in Stensia casually identifies its owner as Edgar Markov, Sorin’s grandfather. The guide also connects Edgar to the ritual that gave rise to Innistrad’s original 12 vampire bloodlines.

The horrifying details came in 2014’s “The Lunarch’s Journal,” an in-universe story published on Magic's website in which a church official discovers that a then-human Edgar worked with the demon Shilgengar to devise a formula for vampirism. The key ingredient was the blood of a living angel. Edgar and his sons trapped the angel Marycz in his laboratory and drained her blood. This revelation is enough to shake the Lunarch’s faith, because the monsters that his church exists to fight were created by humans to begin with.

It has been revealed that the 2016 Dungeons & Dragons supplement Plane Shift: Innistrad explains what Edgar was after. He was an aging alchemist and healer who wanted to prolong his life and the lives of his family. When alchemy didn’t work, he turned to black magic, and Shilgengar offered him a way to live forever. Edgar’s Commander 2017 profile singles out Sorin as one of the people he wanted to save.

In a flashback in 2021’s Innistrad: Crimson Vow story, Sorin remembers standing in front of his family with a cup of blood in his hands. Marycz was still alive, hanging upside down in chains, and she looked at him as if begging him for help. His family held him down, and Edgar forced Sorin to drink. The trauma of becoming a vampire ignited Sorin’s planeswalker spark. He would go on to create Avacyn, the angel Innistrad’s humans worshipped as their protector.

Sources indicate that in a 2020 episode of principal designer Gavin Verhey’s YouTube channel, Good Morning Magic, Verhey explains that, while working on the Vampiric Bloodlust deck for Commander 2017, he asked Kelly Digges on Magic’s creative team who should be its Commander. Digges suggested Edgar. The fit was obvious. If the whole deck was about getting a bunch of vampires onto the battlefield, who better to lead it than the man who’d sired so many of them in the first place?

According to recent reports, the design team initially called the ability that became Eminence “Coach” during playtesting (because a coach helps from the sidelines). An early Edgar was a six-mana 5/5 with an activated ability that cost three more mana to put a +1/+1 counter on each vampire that had attacked that turn. At another point he was a five-mana 4/3. The final Edgar landed at six mana for a 4/4 with first strike and haste. Now, all he has to do is attack to give every vampire you control a +1/+1 counter. That’s a tremendous payoff for a vampire deck, but Edgar goes even further.

It has been revealed that edgar Markov’s Eminence ability is where he gets truly game-breaking. Whenever you cast another vampire spell, Edgar creates a 1/1 black vampire token as long as he’s in the Command Zone or on the battlefield. Even if that spell is countered, the casting trigger still creates the token. After a board wipe, your next vampire spell can get the army going again. And because Eminence is active even while Edgar is in the Command Zone, he cannot be targeted by any spell until you cast him. It’s a perfectly feasible strategy to never actually play Edgar for that very reason. But because his Eminence ability is available from the Command Zone and can be difficult to interact with, that’s not exactly fair or fun to play against.

Wizards had already tested a version of this with Oloro, Ageless Ascetic in Commander 2013. Oloro could sit in the Command Zone and give you two life every turn. Oloro’s ability buys you time, and with the right lifegain combos, it can be very powerful. Edgar’s tokens do the opposite. Every extra vampire can attack, grow with counters, or even get sacrificed for some other benefit. The cheaper they are, the better. It’s positively overwhelming to the point that years after Edgar Markov’s creation, Verhey himself called Eminence a “design mistake” in an interview​​​​​​​ with Magic content creator Ben Bateman.

As Verhey himself explained in a TikTok​​​​​​​ video from June of this year, not all Eminence abilities are created equal. Commander 2017 included three other precons, each with an Eminence Commander focused on creature types. There’s the cat-focused Arahbo, Roar of the World; the wizard-focused ​​​Inalla, Archmage Ritualist; and The Ur-Dragon, who is the progenitor of all dragons in the multiverse. Verhey specifically pointed out that a lot of people complain about Edgar — but nobody complains about Arahbo.

Recent findings suggest that from a design standpoint, that’s because Edgar generates value in the form of more vampires. The others don’t generate additional creatures in the same way.​​​​​​​ Arahbo requires that you already have a cat on the battlefield that it buffs for a single turn. Inalla allows you to pay one mana to copy a nontoken wizard you play, but those copies get exiled at the end of your turn. The Ur-Dragon, also the third-most popular Commander on EDHREC, boasts​​​​​​​ all five colors and reduces the cost of other Dragon spells from the Command Zone​​​​​​​. As Verhey implies in that same video, it’s basically impossible to design a dragon Commander that’s better than The Ur-Dragon.

Industry observers note that edgar Markov’s Eminence ability might be broken, but Eminence itself isn’t gone from Wizards of the Coast’s design toolkit. The Reality Fracture Commander precon includes The Ur-Sphinx, which simply discounts​​​​​​​ all sphinx spells by one mana (a cheeky reference to The Ur-Dragon).

One of my opponents when I participated in a Mystery Booster Commander Edition draft event at MagicCon: Atlanta was also running Sahir, Visitor in Darkness. This fresh card features an Eminence ability that pings its controller for one damage each turn, but when he’s in play, his second ability gives him a +1/+1 counter every time you self-inflict one point of damage. If that happens a second time on any given turn, you draw a card. That makes his Eminence ability a weakness, but if you can counterbalance that with some lifegain effects and manipulate more pings, you’ve got a consistent draw engine.

According to recent reports, early leaks for the upcoming Nauctis: The Sunken Realm have also teased The Ignoble Serpent from a Commander precon that dabbles in an Eminence-esque ability, milling four cards on your first turn. This turns Eminence into a one-time ability to start the game, rather than something that's always on and impossible to interact with. Once The Ignoble Serpent hits the board, it’s a 7/9 that costs eight mana and returns a sea monster from your graveyard to the battlefield on your end step.

The trick when it comes to Eminence, then, is to ensure that these abilities have some kind of drawback so that they’re not as overpowered as they are with Edgar Markov, while still feeding into some kind of core strategy.

Still, nothing beats the elegant simplicity of hitting your opponents with a massive vampire storm while your vampire lord coaches them from the sidelines.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After slamming the brakes on more than 1,800 data center projects in August, Texas has once again started approving them following a upcoming directive from outgoing Republican governor Greg Abbott's office.
  • It has been revealed that as recently as October, Texas suspended a further 17 data center construction permits and shut down an automated portal that was found to still be approving upcoming permits.
  • In a recent development, but even with ERCOT's investigation complete, the processing of new power requests isn't one that is expected to happen promptly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After slamming the brakes on more than 1,800 data center projects in August, Texas has once again started approving them following a upcoming directive from outgoing Republican governor Greg Abbott's office. The move came after the same office also paused the approval of permits, saying that Abbot's "top priority is to protect Texans’ safety and quality of life” amid concerns over the amount of power new data centers would require. At the time, the move meant that 474 gigawatts of new power requests became subject to the moratorium. But with Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa's January arrival edging ever closer, Abbott has done a 180-degree pivot, with the FT reporting that data center builders are rushing to get their approvals in before the new governor arrives. Hinojosa has already pledged to rein in new data center construction.

It has been revealed that as recently as October, Texas suspended a further 17 data center construction permits and shut down an automated portal that was found to still be approving upcoming permits. That system will surely be switched back on now that Abbott's office has confirmed that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which is in charge of the state’s electrical grid, has finished gathering the information that it needed on how data centers affect local communities.

In a recent development, but even with ERCOT's investigation complete, the processing of new power requests isn't one that is expected to happen promptly. With that in mind, some developers have already taken matters into their own hands, choosing to build their own power centers to reduce or eliminate their reliance on the local grid. The region's large gas supplies are helping this effort, as is what is considered to be a "lax" regulatory environment. This all means that the possibility of using gas turbines to power new data centers is a viable one, although some are looking beyond traditional gas-powered options. In Mississippi, Elon Musk's xAI installed eight converted jet engines to power its data center, despite the known health risks posed by their use.

It has been revealed that while it remains to be seen what impact the arrival of incoming Governor Hinojosa will have on data centers in the area, there's little doubt that they will be a hot topic. Locals continue to be concerned about the environmental impact these facilities have, while increased costs associated with powering their own homes are another problem. Texas isn't alone in facing these problems, with New York announcing a year-long ban on data center projects larger than 50 megawatts that came into force earlier this year. In Northern Virginia, Amazon abandoned plans to build four new data centers after public outcry. The land will now be used for housing instead.

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Nvidia agrees to $290 million settlement over 2018 crypto mining GPU sales

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Tomshardware)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia has agreed to pay a $290 million settlement in an eight-year-long securities class action lawsuit.
  • 2017-2018 were some of the most rampant years for cryptocurrency mining, with plenty of scalpers buying up the Pascal GTX 1000-Series GPUs released in early 2017.
  • Recent findings suggest that when the 2018 crypto crash hit, Nvidia’s revenue felt it too, with a sharp decline in gaming sales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia has agreed to pay a $290 million settlement in an eight-year-long securities class action lawsuit. Investors accused the tech giant of misleading shareholders about how much of its gaming revenue was actually driven by the cryptocurrency mining boom in 2018.

2017-2018 were some of the most rampant years for cryptocurrency mining, with plenty of scalpers buying up the Pascal GTX 1000-Series GPUs released in early 2017. Nvidia also sold the P106-100 that year, a dedicated cryptocurrency mining GPU with similar hardware to the GTX 1060, and it was attributed to OEM sales. Many gamers remember how scarce retail gaming GPUs were in those years, yet Huang stated in November 2017 that what cryptocurrency contributes is “small but not zero,” as highlighted in the Summary of Alleged False and Misleading Statements section of the March court filing.

Recent findings suggest that when the 2018 crypto crash hit, Nvidia’s revenue felt it too, with a sharp decline in gaming sales. The plaintiffs saw this strong correlation, seeing how cryptocurrency demand closely followed gaming GPU sales. The litigation states that Nvidia was “forced to partially reveal the truth on August 16, 2018, when it lowered their revenue guidance and acknowledged that ‘a great deal’ of cryptocurrency miners had bought GeForce Gaming GPUs.” Following the admissions, Nvidia’s stock price also fell 28.5% over two trading sessions.

After the crash, Nvidia struggled with excess inventory, with CFO Colette Kress stating that “Gaming was short of expectations as post-crypto channel inventory took longer than expected to sell through,” painting a clearer picture of how much crypto impacted Nvidia’s sales, which were allegedly attributed to gaming sales. It’s unclear how much of those gaming sales were from cryptocurrency mining, but considering that an overwhelming amount of retail gaming GPUs were bought out by cryptocurrency miners, it’s reasonable to say it’s difficult to keep track of who purchased and for what purpose.

Recent findings suggest that in 2021, the district court dismissed the lawsuit, but part of the dismissal was reversed by the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, reviving the lawsuit and allowing the securities fraud claims against Nvidia to proceed. Nvidia still denies wrongdoing, but has decided to settle, agreeing with the plaintiffs to pay $290 million in September, according to the Tuesday court filing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Kioxia Corporation showcased a prototype of its latest XL-Flash Generation 3 technology, next-generation low-latency, high-performance flash memory, at its KIOXIA Forum in Tokyo. The flash, which uses CMOS directly Bonded to Array, or CBA, for better power efficiency and storage density, is about 135% more efficient with 70% higher bit density than Gen 2, and its 3 µs average read latency is less than 10% of that of Kioxia’s standard BiCS8 TLC. Samples are due March 2027, and Kioxia named its GP2 enterprise SSDs, rated for more than 18 million 512-byte random read IOPS, as its first product using it.

The low-latency XL-Flash fills “a latest memory tier” to bridge the gap between DRAM and regular flash memory, in a way that can complement or replace some DRAM to help drive down costs, especially in AI servers and data centers. This has some similarities to Optane, which used 3D XPoint instead, as a storage class memory (SCM) option to reach higher IOPS. Intel and Micron’s 3D XPoint stored bits as changes in the cell material’s resistance rather than as trapped charge like NAND, and Intel exited the Optane business in 2022. The XL-Flash NAND is built on BiCS flash technology, but it’s tuned for low read latency and high write endurance.

The first generation was SLC with under-5 µs reads, arriving in 2019. By 2022, Gen 2 added 2-bit MLC as an option for lower bit cost, trading some like-for-like performance for better price-to-density. Gen 3 is reported to use SLC, and its 3 µs average read latency challenges the first gen’s sub-5 µs rating while being more than ten times faster than the 40 µs of standard BiCS8 TLC. This is within the same ballpark as Optane SSDs. The flash also reportedly has SLC endurance at 150,000 to 250,000 P/E cycles, at least 50x standard TLC, running at a 4.8 Gb/s interface speed.

under 5 µs (SLC), under 10 µs (MLC).

XL-Flash achieves lower latency, in part, by using more, smaller planes (16 per die, with a 4KB page, on earlier generations), which is common with SLC and low-latency flash, and especially helps with smaller I/O. Kioxia’s GP drives target 512B accesses rather than the typical 4KB, a pattern that matches developments in enterprise storage requirements for AI and other emerging workloads that involve constant fine-grained memory lookups. 3D XPoint would outmatch it for write performance, though, due to not needing to erase for upcoming data.

In a recent development, the newer gen is able to maintain high levels of performance at much higher density thanks to CBA bonding, where Kioxia makes the logic CMOS wafer and flash memory-cell wafer separately and later bonds them. This technology also improves the efficiency of 512-byte reads, by Kioxia’s own tests, which matches the design intention of the forthcoming GP2. Kioxia hasn’t disclosed full details on the flash, such as layer count.

The GP2 Super High IOPS SSD will be Kioxia’s first product to use the new flash, promising high levels of performance, including up to 28 GB/s sequential reads, if it can saturate PCIe 6.0 x4 as expected. Kioxia’s 2.5x IOPS number, versus “typical TLC-based SSDs,” comes from a comparison to its own CM10 drives, for 512B I/O. Endurance will also be excellent at up to 50 drive writes per day, which is within the ballpark of Optane storage.

Kioxia is considering E1.S and E3.S form factors, and the drive will support direct liquid cooling, which is increasingly necessary for certain data centers, including GPU-heavy ones where the GP2 is likely to operate.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Recent findings suggest that these drives will serve as a flash tier to help get more out of a GPU’s HBM, and Kioxia first indicated the GP series with Nvidia earlier this year. Offloading memory by any means possible is becoming a strategy with AI, even at the enthusiast level, due to high memory demands and how the technology and its KV caching work.

In a recent development, while the flash should sample to select customers before the end of the first quarter of 2027, Kioxia only promises GP2 evaluation samples to select customers by the end of that year. Exact specifications for the drive may differ, but what is clear is that later GP drives will target up to 100 million random-read IOPS that Kioxia and Nvidia have been working toward for AI servers. Kioxia revealed its XL1 series of CXL memory expansion modules on XL-Flash in August, and it “will continue to leverage the speed, power efficiency, and endurance of XL-FLASH” for emerging data center needs.

#632. Latest Update: AMD and Winbond vulnerabilities let attackers brute-force BitLocker PINs on millions of PCs

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (962 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: AMD and Winbond vulnerabilities let attackers brute-force BitLocker PINs on millions of PCs

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Tomshardware)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former owners of laptops gained yet another concern today.
  • It has been revealed that the paper covers many vulnerabilities, but we'll focus on the big three.
  • It has been revealed that an attacker makes brute-forcing easier by resetting, or pretending to increase, the counter that records the number of failed unlock attempts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former owners of laptops gained yet another concern today. Firmware-backed drive encryption setups like Windows' BitLocker are meant to protect against someone stealing your laptop or desktop computer. Prospective thieves would have a hard time guessing your PIN, as they'll eventually have to wait 10 minutes for each attempt. That is, unless your machine uses a modern AMD CPU or relies on Winbond's SPI flash — in which case your data may be open for inspection in a few days, or even hours, as researchers from Technische Universität Berlin found out.

It has been revealed that the paper covers many vulnerabilities, but we'll focus on the big three. All focus on having a way to brute-force an encrypted drive's password in a matter of days/hours rather than years. Physical access is required for the attacks, but hardware theft is precisely the scenario that disk encryption is meant to protect against.

It has been revealed that an attacker makes brute-forcing easier by resetting, or pretending to increase, the counter that records the number of failed unlock attempts. On Intel- and AMD-based PCs using the fTPM for security — nearly all modern x86 consumer machines — this counter is stored encrypted in an SPI flash chip on the motherboard.

Standard procedure is to allow for 32 attempts in succession, then force the machine to wait 10 minutes for each additional one, resulting in many years for unlocking a short PIN — 19 years for a six-digit numerical PIN, under normal conditions. We should note the attacks likely extend to other fTPM-based disk encryption mechanisms, not just BitLocker. While encryption keys can be alphanumeric, Microsoft Windows does default to using a numeric PIN for sign-in, and most users don't use long ones.

First up: machines based on Winbond's RPMC-enabled SPI flash (variant with rollback protection), used by many OEMs across both Intel and AMD platforms. Although it's hard to pin down the number of affected machines, the paper claims Winbond has roughly a 25% market share for SPI flash — so, potentially millions of machines. With a simple voltage glitch, the researchers made the chip reveal the HMAC key, the datum that signs commands when the TPM and the SPI chip talk to each other.

Industry observers note that with the HMAC in hand, the thief places a low-cost interposer board in front of the SPI chip to impersonate it. On a failed unlock, the computer will request a counter increase and get a confirmation, when in reality nothing happened — allowing for repeat attempts as fast as Windows lets them, at five per reboot. There is no fix for this vulnerability other than replacing the SPI chip with one that doesn't contain the bug.

The team glitched two specific Winbond chip models, but they theorize the matter extends further into the maker's lineup, as the flaw allegedly lies with the RPMC engine design. Flash chips from other firms in the test were not affected to the same extent.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, as for AMD machines, the situation is both worse and better, with two related vulnerabilities. The team verified at least one of the two attacks across AMD machines from Zen 2 up to an AI 5 330 laptop. They theorize that considering the mechanisms, all contemporary AMD setups may be vulnerable, at least for standard consumer hardware using fTPM. That's multiple millions of machines potentially at risk, on the low side.

In a recent development, the first is simple enough. On the tested machines whose SPI flash didn't use RPMC — rollback protection — you can just make a copy of the SPI flash's contents when the counter is low, and just flash it again once you've used up your free tries. Bad enough, yes, but the second vulnerability should elicit facepalms from security architects.

According to the paper, AMD's firmware controller for non-volatile storage — the bit that talks to the SPI flash — does not verify that the failed-attempt counter increase actually took place. It'll just problem the order to +1 it and be done, opening the avenue for an attacker to simply intercept that order (again, with a cheap board) and ignore it without even needing HMAC keys, so the counter never changes.

The latter vulnerability should be fixable via a firmware revision, almost certainly via AMD's AGESA software. The problem is one of practicality: in the past, updating AGESA on client hardware meant that every OEM had to create fresh BIOSes for affected machines, many of which are assuredly out of their support window.

Anyone who's lived through the Spectre and Meltdown days knows how hard it is in practice, as OEMs are exceedingly slow to publish updates, and have a distaste for providing fixes for hardware that's more than a few years old.

The researchers contacted every company involved in their tests, informing them of their findings, but sadly "none of them has committed to fixing the root-cause vulnerabilities" — at least, as of this writing, only Microsoft unveiled a policy change recommending customers enter six-digit PINs instead of the current four during setup.

Rockstar Games has revealed why players can find chainsaws in GTA 6 but can’t use them as weapons, with producer Rob Nelson saying the studio felt they’d be “too much” for the game.

Both the chainsaw and katana were famously usable in Vice City and San Andreas, letting fans slice and dice their foes for some brutal yet fun takedowns. While Jason and Lucia can spot chainsaws across Leonida, neither can actually pick them up and wield them.

Speaking to VGC, co-studio head at Rockstar North Rob Nelson remarked the decision came down to how chainsaw violence would look in GTA 6 and whether it fit the game’s two protagonists.

In a recent development, “As far as the chainsaw, I think it would have been too much for this game at this resolution and these characters. It’s not a resource thing, noted Nelson.

“Even at the most psycho, did Jason and Lucia really need that, what’s that going to look like?”.

After all, GTA 6 is the most hyper-realistic open-world game Rockstar has created to date. Its fictional world of Florida is absolutely crammed with environmental details, wildlife, and NPCs all going about their business.

Nelson said Rockstar wanted players to interact with as much of the world as possible, but had to weigh what each of those interactions would add to the game.

“You’re always trying to find what is the right sort of line and the right balance, it really just depends, you want to feel like you can interact with as much of the world as possible.”.

Recent findings suggest that that same question of what fits Jason and Lucia came up when Nelson explained why Rockstar added GTA 6’s Criminal Profile system. As previously reported, Rockstar wanted what players do in the open world to better reflect how the pair are portrayed in the story, while giving players more ways to handle everyday encounters.

Sources indicate that for example, players can rob someone at gunpoint and give them a chance to hand over their money. Meanwhile, repeated acts of extreme violence can permanently lock a character’s Criminal Profile at Irredeemable, which drastically impacts how aggressively police respond to your actions.

According to recent reports, if you're looking at wiring up your home or figuring out your entire networking situation, nothing ever beats being plugged into an Ethernet port. The TP-Link LS1005G Lightwave 5-port unmanaged Ethernet switch is back down to its lowest-ever price at just $7.99 on Amazon as a part of their Black Friday sale. At over 53% off, an unmanaged switch buys you freedom and, crucially, more Ethernet ports to play around with. This device is ideal for those looking to connect essential devices via Ethernet, like networked cameras, an office full of electronics, or a multi-system homelab setup.

In a recent development, when the switch is this cheap, it's difficult to overstate how useful it could be if you're a resident tinkerer like any of us on the Tom's Hardware staff team. Each port can deliver full gigabit speeds across a 10Gbps backplane on the switch. That means if you're running a rapid setup, you'll still get gigabit-level speeds across all devices that are connected to this unit.

It's also useful for those who have mesh networks, with only one single Ethernet port coming out of a satellite node. This unmanaged switch will give you access to more ports and more wired devices without the pitfalls of hooking things up over Wi-Fi, which can be prone to interference or latency. In this scenario, though, you're ideally looking at the satellite node running a wired backhaul across your network to maintain stability and avoid pitfalls like packet loss.

The TP-Link Litewave 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet Switch LS1005G provides four additional Ethernet ports, delivering reliable, high-speed wired internet for your gaming PC, NAS, console, TV, and other connected devices.

Given the price, it's important to note what you don't get with an inexpensive, unmanaged switch such as this. You won't receive any Power over Ethernet on the LS1005G switch, so if your networked cameras rely on it, you should look elsewhere. Additionally, as it's unmanaged, you cannot... well... manage it. Strictly speaking, 1Gbps should be more than enough bandwidth for most at-home use cases, such as NAS systems or sending files across your network. But if you're regularly sending larger files and have the infrastructure to support it, then looking at a unit with faster ports might be worthwhile for you, but if you don't think you'll hit the gigabit ceiling often, it's a perfect set-and-forget device.

Industry observers note that in particular, for the gamers among you, gigabit ports will be more than stable enough to support online gaming, even in titles that demand no packet loss, like online Rollback netcode in competitive fighting games like Street Fighter 6 and Fatal Fury: City of the Wolves. Remember, sustaining the harmony of a wired network does have its benefits! At under $8 on Amazon, TP-Link's unmanaged switch fits a huge variety of use cases and is also just handy to keep around, in case you'll need one later down the line.

TSMC gives a sneap peak at AI Design Kit: Agentic AI with foundry expertise

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Tomshardware)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the semiconductor industry is in a paradoxical situation these days.
  • At its 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop in Munich, TSMC this week unveiled its AI Design Kit (ADK), a collection of process-specific technical information, implementation guidelines, and design methodologies that enables AI agents to automate and optimize chip development flows.
  • Industry observers note that the ADK complements the foundry's traditional process design kits (PDKs) and enables AI agents to use TSMC's process-specific expertise, knowledge of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, and customers' proprietary design methodologies to automate physical implementation and optimization of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the semiconductor industry is in a paradoxical situation these days. On the one hand, AI drives demand for the leading-edge nodes from both established players and new entrants, with everyone trying to accelerate the development cycle. On the other hand, leading-edge nodes become more complex, which increases entry barriers and stretches design cycles. While the challenge seems to be insoluble, it looks like TSMC has found a solution.

At its 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop in Munich, TSMC this week unveiled its AI Design Kit (ADK), a collection of process-specific technical information, implementation guidelines, and design methodologies that enables AI agents to automate and optimize chip development flows.

Industry observers note that the ADK complements the foundry's traditional process design kits (PDKs) and enables AI agents to use TSMC's process-specific expertise, knowledge of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, and customers' proprietary design methodologies to automate physical implementation and optimization of chips. Ultimately, the initiative aims to reduce development cycles, improve design productivity, and simplify adoption of TSMC's advanced process technologies.

Recent findings suggest that "The ADK complements our traditional PDK, and it brings in capabilities to augment the EDA and other design flows," said Aveek Sarkar, Head of Ecosystem and Alliance Management at TSMC. "Our goal with these agentic flows is to bring in the technology-specific learning we have at TSMC and layer that with your orchestration layer, with your design expertise, and to support the next generation of EDA or design flows and methodologies that you have.".

Sources indicate that while every upcoming fabrication process from TSMC offers advantages in terms of power, performance, and area (PPA), it also considerably increases design complexity. Compared to TSMC's N5-derived manufacturing technologies (including various N4 nodes), the number of design rules has increased by 2.3X with N3P, 3.1X with N2P, and 3.6X with A14 (the first node to be supported by the ADK).

In a recent development, meanwhile, the number of available standard library cells has increased by 2.8X, 5X, and 4.6X, respectively. Add to that a greater number of metallization stack options and plenty of EDA tool settings, and the number of possible design configurations becomes massive. As a result, conventional design optimization methodologies approach their productivity limits, according to TSMC. At the same time, some of TSMC's customers want to reduce their chip development cycles from 18 months to 12 months, Sarkar stated.

In a recent development, usage of agentic AI could help chip developers to explore more design configurations within shorter timeframes, achieve more favorable PPA results from advanced process technologies, and potentially improve manufacturability and yields by implementing more extensive physical design optimization. Furthermore, it could reduce the amount of engineering work required to adopt a new fabrication process for a new design.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

"AI is bringing a significant benefit: faster design cycles, more verification coverage, faster time to closure," Sarkar said.

TSMC's early-phase AI Design Kit incorporates process-specific information, such as metal pitches, standard cell heights, routing track patterns, library cell naming conventions, and implementation guidelines, according to slides demonstrated at the event.

With the ADK, EDA agents — such as Cadence's InnoStack or Synopsys's Implementation Agent — can use a simple natural-language prompt and a large language model (LLM) to automatically generate a qualified automatic placement and routing (APR) reference flow for TSMC's A14 process technology. Such a flow includes project setup, library cell usage, placement and routing optimization, routing track and power grid creation, and wide-wire configuration. Traditionally, engineers could spend weeks on preparation of such scripts, but now APR scripts could be prepped with a natural language prompt, though TSMC did not disclose the actual time it takes to prep them (probably because it depends on design complexity and goals).

"Instead of spending weeks preparing APR scripts, EDA agents can take a simple prompt from customers and the TSMC ADK and use a generative model to deliver a qualified APR reference flow," a spokesperson from TSMC noted at the stage.

For more sophisticated design tasks, TSMC proposes an orchestration agent that resides at the customer's site and combines three sources of knowledge with clear ownership:.

The orchestrator coordinates agents responsible for design diagnostics, power grid implementation, timing closure, design rule checks, and congestion mitigation. These agents analyze EDA tool output and automatically adjust parameters for subsequent iterations across floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis, routing, sign-off, and engineering change orders (ECOs). Such a methodology enables continuous design optimization 24/7 with less human intervention.

Industry observers note that "The orchestrator then directs these agents to analyze the output of EDA tools and automatically adjust the settings for the next iteration across floorplan, placement, CTS, routing, sign-off, and ECO," the spokesman stated. "This agentic AI flow drives the iterative design process 24/7, minimizing the turnaround time and maximizing productivity.".

For now, TSMC's ADK primarily addresses physical implementation rather than chip architecture or logic design. The company has not demonstrated an autonomous design flow that takes a chip from an architectural specification to tape-out without human intervention. Nor has TSMC disclosed quantified PPA improvements, actual reductions in development cycles, or a commercial availability timeframe for its ADK.

It is noteworthy that TSMC's ADK neither replaces conventional PDKs nor substitutes for advanced AI-enabled EDA software from Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens EDA, or other developers. Instead, it provides process-specific knowledge that enables AI agents to make more informed decisions, while the actual physical implementation, simulation, optimization, and verification tasks remain the domain of specialized EDA tools. Thus, chip developers cannot use the ADK independently of traditional EDA infrastructure.

In a recent development, for TSMC, the ADK could accelerate adoption of its latest fabrication processes, as customers could adapt their design methodologies to new nodes faster. Smaller fabless chip developers could also gain access to sophisticated physical design methodologies without the need to develop expertise comparable to that of prominent chip developers entirely in-house. Meanwhile, EDA and IP providers could benefit from closer integration of their products into process-specific design flows, whereas contract chip designers could offer shorter development times for their customers without significant additional investments.

There is also a potential customer lock-in aspect. While TSMC's proposed architecture preserves customers' ownership of proprietary design knowledge, extensive integration of foundry-specific physical design enablement collateral, EDA agents, and internal orchestration systems could make migration to another foundry harder and generally less likely as chipmakers get more accustomed to TSMC ADK (which is an exclusive capability for now and will remain an exclusive offering for a while). In effect, TSMC's competitive advantages will extend well beyond its process technologies, production capabilities, and conventional design ecosystem to include intelligence that emphasizes its customers' chip development methodologies.

Rockstar boss "so grateful" to have kept GTA 6's big prologue twist a secret - and reveals Tomás' story could have been very different

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Eurogamer)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you've played the first 20 minutes or so of Grand Theft Auto 6, you'll know there's a hugely significant plot revelation there - one Rockstar somehow managed to keep entirely secret until the game's launch.
  • According to recent reports, it's somewhat miraculous they did, given the many leaks the studio has suffered until now.
  • Speaking to Eurogamer in an interview shortly before GTA 6 was released, Rockstar Games' head of development Rob Nelson discussed the secret and, notably, the fact the team also discussed going another way entirely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've played the first 20 minutes or so of Grand Theft Auto 6, you'll know there's a hugely significant plot revelation there - one Rockstar somehow managed to keep entirely secret until the game's launch.

According to recent reports, it's somewhat miraculous they did, given the many leaks the studio has suffered until now. And while, frankly, the embargo restrictions around discussing it in our GTA 6 review made a deeper analysis of Jason and Lucia's story more than a little awkward, I'm also mostly glad it remained a surprise. It's one of the great twists delivered in a game of this kind.

Speaking to Eurogamer in an interview shortly before GTA 6 was released, Rockstar Games' head of development Rob Nelson discussed the secret and, notably, the fact the team also discussed going another way entirely.

Spoilers for GTA 6's opening half hour - and further backstory around that moment from later in the game - below.

The big twist of course is that Jason and Lucia have a young child, Tomás, who we see Lucia abandoning in order to rob a store at gunpoint during the game's prologue.

Recent findings suggest that it's an astonishing moment, both in the complexity it immediately lends Lucia, who is at once painted in a more negative light as a result, and in the stakes it affords her and Jason. This is the first time GTA's protagonists have genuine, human stakes that underpin their actions during the game's story, and at the same time Rockstar, in doing so, opens a route for itself to offering a far more nuanced take on modern crime.

But it was also something of a risk – and a hotly debated one, as Nelson told me during our conversation – as giving the game's protagonists that kind of narrative weight ran somewhat counter to the crime movie, straight-to-the-action thrills of previous GTAs.

In a recent development, "I'm so grateful that we managed to keep that under wraps," Nelson stated. The subversion of expectations was intentional. "You feel like you maybe know these characters, or what the game or the story is going to be about, and then in the first 10, 15 minutes, it takes on a completely different context."It was an idea that came about organically. "But the idea of the character wanting something that maybe is at odds with what you thought you wanted as a player coming in, which is amassing as much material wealth as possible, and as many cars, and as many things," he said, was something Rockstar found particularly compelling.

Recent findings suggest that the next point of the studio's focus then became the justification for Lucia's decision, Nelson explained. "The story was always, broadly, going to go through some of the major beats that it did," once Rockstar decided on the key points of the protagonists being a couple and them having a child. "But the details of the relationship, the narrative details of it, we dialled in a lot - because we're doing a lot there. She's leaving a kid early on – that's not a very sympathetic move to make.".

Industry observers note that that led to the decision to show, later in the story, more about why Lucia opted to leave Tomás in that moment. "Many chapters later, where [Jason] is like: 'What? Why did you do that?' And she has a flashback to sort of being at her wit's end," Nelson stated, which then flows into the question of why she left Jason in the first place. "Cal asks Jason, 'Why did she leave?' And so, well, she didn't know she was pregnant at the time. 'Okay, but why didn't she call you?' 'Well, because I might've told her I didn't want [to be a father].' So you have to just make sure that you can understand both of their perspectives.".

The tension from the fact they had a child, and that the two of them were away from their son as you play the game, was significant enough to become a point of discussion within the studio.

In a recent development, "Multiple times throughout development, we had this child, and people are like, 'Can it not be, like, theirs?'" Nelson mentioned. "'Could it be like her little sister? Could it be– because I really feel bad having a good time in Vice City…' and the questions are valid," he continued. "But it wouldn't be powerful if not. So it was up to us to figure out how [you resolve that tension].".

Industry observers note that like with Lucia's justification for leaving Tomás - revealed in a striking dream-slash-flashback later in the game, that mixes typically exaggerated Rockstar satire with genuine social commentary - this then led to a cascade of other character moments. "How about he's in a better position than he would ever be with them, and so he's with her aunt, who's way more stable, and has a loving husband and other little kids, and he's always having a good time?" Nelson mentioned.

According to recent reports, he points to a conversation between Jason and Lucia in the game's first chapter as another example. "Very early on, in chapter one, they have this chat where he's like, 'Let's FaceTime - FruitFace is the thing we use - and she's like, 'No, I don't want to confuse him. He's better off until we get our shit together.' And he's like 'Okay' and she's like, 'It's not a cop-out', and he's like, 'No, no, I met my father on the other side of a glass divider, so I'm kind of trying to break that cycle.' And that's right in chapter one, and so it's a thread all the way through.".

The result, then, is that the decision to add Tomás ultimately shaped many of the key parts of Jason and Lucia's characters, from their relationships with their own parents – Jason's being in jail, and Lucia's mother too narcissistic to help – to what is, really, the entire narrative arc of the story. And rightly so; a child is a big deal, and one of many reasons why GTA 6 is able to tap into something deeper than any of the previous games in the series before.

We've much more from our interview with Rob Nelson to come over the following days. In the meantime, he discussed why Rockstar made a form of honour system a core part of GTA 6's design (spoiler: because thinking more deeply about your in-game choices is fun). And in other Rockstar news, the studio has surprised those keeping up with its ongoing unionisation efforts by voting against formal recognition of the Rockstar Game Workers' Union.

Naturally, Instagram owners were delighted by the news, with the post attracting more than 41,000 likes.

  • The practice of exploiting warlocks in this way is called summon-kicking, and aside from the in-game reporting feature, there is little recourse to admonish such behavior.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Being recruited to a World of Warcraft party as a warlock, only to be swiftly kicked again after using your powers to magically summon the party members together in the same place, may soon become a thing of the past. All thanks to a mod made by one especially peeved warlock.

The practice of exploiting warlocks in this way is called summon-kicking, and aside from the in-game reporting feature, there is little recourse to admonish such behavior.

Enter Summoners Union, the add-on mod, which grants the ability to flag and track players who summon-kick thereby building a collective case against them.

It has been revealed that the mod was showcased on the World of Warcraft: Forever Reddit by user 274Moons, highlighting its ability to flag players after they boot you from a party, but also that it warns you if anyone in the party has a record of summon-kicking. It can also be combined with an in-game chat channel where warlock comrades can pull together and discuss and ultimately maybe fend off this nasty behavior.

Industry observers note that "I play a lock and got tired of the usual 'hey can you summon?', ten minutes at the stone, last person comes through, *You have been removed from the group.*," 274Moons wrote. "So I made an addon about it. It's called The Summoners Union.".

In a recent development, according to the add-on's creator, over 500 Warlocks have already downloaded Summon Union. It's a relatively small number in comparison to the wider World of Warcraft: Forever population, but it's a notable start.

"Thank you for this, I hate being just a taxi," wrote user Gregore997. Others also were quick to thank 274Moons for their service to all the Warlocks out there, such as Nangz who wrote: "Please keep the community sharing!".

World of Warcraft: Forever has been out for a little while now and it's been received rather well, breaking records for the series in terms of active players. The playerbase is currently awaiting the release of the game's first raids next month.

In a recent development, when Rockstar Games confirmed that Grand Theft Auto 6 would initially only be released on consoles, PC players were left disappointed. Many hoped that, unlike Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 5, they wouldn’t have to wait a long time for the PC port.

According to recent reports, however, there have been some attempts to get an unofficial version of the game working on PC, since leakers have gotten the game’s source code. Rockstar has shut down a Discord server that had managed to get GTA 6 booting on PC, even though it didn’t progress past the Rockstar logo screen.

Now, though, some PC players have a “working” multiplayer system in GTA 6, including proximity chat.

It was highlighted by Developer TeK, who showed a lobby with two people at once. In a short video, the two met up at the airport, driving cars towards each other and interacting.

Sources indicate that as per the developer, this unofficial port is running at 25–30 FPS. PortWatch, a community tracker for unofficial GTA 6 ports, confirmed that the footage is genuine, but has not yet verified the FPS.

They noted it is on a “private build” and “nobody outside the group” has access to it.

Recent findings suggest that GTA VI Working Multiplayer, Character, Vehicles & Proximity voice chat. (25-30FPS)#GTAVI #GTA6 pic.twitter.com/PyWvg764zZ.

Social media people believe that the unofficial ports are opening modders up to an “unholy legal sh*tstorm” that could affect the entire modding community.

In a recent development, “This ruins gaming idc,” another said. “This s*it is why everything will be digital and behind subscriptions,” another added. “At this rate, Claude is gonna get serious guardrails,” another chimed in.

Take-Two has warned modders who want to release an unofficial port, noting that they’ve been “enhancing our legal activities” around it.

It has been revealed that there have been reports that an official PC version will be released in early 2027, with GTA Online in GTA 6 apparently slated for “next year” as well. Twitch CEO Dan Clancy said he’d had conversations with Rockstar about the multiplayer release.

Take-Two has also stated they will support the current iteration of GTA Online for as long as players want to stick around.

According to recent reports, for 16 years I've been watching the skies. It was 16 years ago, back in the first giddy rush of smartphone gaming, that I saw a 30-second trailer for a game set in space. It was a game about a comet, hurtling through the unknown. It wasn't clear what you'd do in this game, whether you'd control the comet itself or the space it moved through. It wasn't clear if this was some kind of arcade game, or a new spin on the endless runner, or even just a kind of cosmic sandbox. All I had was the comet and a name: Faraway. Faraway! I was captivated.

Faraway is one of those wonderfully cludged together childhood words, like "nonesuch". Where is the edge of the galaxy? Oh, it's faraway. Where is the edge of the universe? Oh, there's nonesuch thing.

It has been revealed that okay, Faraway came with one other bit of info I could cling to at the time. It was being made by Steph Thirion, a musician and designer and, I sensed, many other things too. At the time Faraway was announced I'd just played his game Eliss, which was an early smartphone hit. In the absence of any more information on Faraway itself, I had to make do with that. Maybe Faraway would be a bit like Eliss?

According to recent reports, eliss itself, though? Oh, boy. This thing is beautiful, frantic, strange, compelling and indescribable. And think what that means, just for a second, for something to be both compelling and indescribable. I am driven to do these things, but I don't really know what these things are. I'm prodding little bits of colour around, maybe planets, maybe molecules? I am combining them, gathering them, turning them into something greater together than they are by themselves?

Last week I spoke to Thirion - as for why, well, we will get to that - and at the start I asked him about Eliss, about how it felt to make a game that was so hard to put into words, and if he actually had any words for it himself.

"I love that question," he laughs. "I guess I would say that for Eliss, it was all about that interaction of moving things, moving those little circles with each of your fingers individually." He pauses, thinking back. "It's not something I had envisioned. I was programming, and I was basically testing touch controls because I was trying to build a different game. But then I was playing with that [stuff]. I was like: that feels really nice. Can I build a game around that? So I guess there is something beyond language about that interaction. I was attracted to it in that way. It wasn't rational. It was a feeling. It feels good.".

It's both thrilling and slightly melancholic to think back to the days of Eliss. Apps were in ascendence, but nobody fully understood them yet. There weren't yet consultants or established monetisation pathways. There wasn't even much agreement on the best ways to approach the touchscreen. Eliss and other weird, memorable, hard-to-talk-about games were all part of this Cambrian explosion. You'd get up in the morning and check socials and there was a new game everyone was enthusing about. There was a new world to get lost in.

"I would say that's true even outside of mobile," Thirion tells me. "Just indies in general. There was a lot of excitement going around and a lot of eyeballs. What are people gonna think about next?" He takes a long breath. "It felt like there's a lot of opportunity for new things and new ideas, and people were excited about that. Everything was set up for innovation. It felt like I was part of something.".

Recent findings suggest that this is the world that Faraway and its comet first emerged from, streaking across a night sky in which any kind of discovery felt possible. "The real genesis was actually just before Eliss," Thirion states. "I was really spending a lot of time thinking about a possible career in video games. I was an interaction designer and programmer doing interactive experiences, mostly for advertising.

"And for some reason, the iPhone was the thing that made me think I could do something on my own, and what I'd like to do is probably video games. So I was I was thinking a lot about that, maybe obsessively, to the point where there was a night that I was in the countryside in France and just looking at the stars and thinking: it would be great to have a video game where you can fly in the sky that I'm looking at, in this 2D firmament, right? That was it.".

The next step towards Faraway came at GDC in 2010, with a call for games that could be controlled with a single button. "I started prototyping," Thirion notes. "I tried a few things, and I had this idea of using this kind of physics-y thing about swinging around stars. It actually worked pretty rapidly.".

Industry observers note that then? Sixteen years pass. What was happening during this time?

Recent findings suggest that it's a long answer with, perhaps, a short answer buried inside it. Let's deal with the long answer first.

"It's not like I worked 16 years on this game," Thirion laughs. He explains that the first prototype was begun in 2010 for the GDC one-button competition. It was playable by March. "That was basically at the beginning," he says. "I was like: This is a very simple game, and I'm just going to put it out in a couple months.".

In a recent development, and after that? "I started to have greater ambitions, and then life happened," he claims. He didn't work on the game for seven years, and then Annapurna Interactive found him and asked him to return to Faraway, offering support. "And so, after that, the journey was to turn [the game] into an audiovisual experience.

Recent findings suggest that "And so I started doing an audiovisual experience, but it was still aesthetically like Ellis: low-resolution pixel art. I had the ambition of taking it to a different language. I basically wanted to make the jump from procedural low-resolution to procedural infinite resolution!" He ended up with a very smooth, almost vector-like aesthetic. It looks beautiful, but it came at a price. "That took a lot of effort," he notes. "Also to make it performant? That required a rewrite of the game into a completely latest engine. It was a new language for me as well, so I had to learn this new language.".

According to recent reports, all of this is extremely convincing, as are a hundred other bumps in the road. It makes sense. I've written about games for twenty years, and my sense is that game development is hard, and that it takes time.

It has been revealed that but there's something else Thirion says. And this makes me wonder if part of the truth as to why Faraway took so long to make is actually a lot simpler, and a lot more human.

In a recent development, "I was thinking a lot about Tetris," Thirion says. "I had just started making video games, and I thought a lot about Tetris because it's a very simple rule set that seems to be compelling whether you're two hours in or 1000 hours in, right? And that's like kind of a rare thing.

Industry observers note that "And at the time we were talking about: are game's art and so on. And I was like, man, to me, Tetris is art. It does something almost impossible. At least now I look at it and I think it does something almost impossible. But at the time, I was like, well, why are games growing in complexity and quantity instead of staying simple and going deep? And so, I was really asking myself the question: where can I find that balance of just being compelling at any skill level with a very minimal rule set, and that kind of took me into this rabbit hole of experimentation.".

According to recent reports, it's hard for me not to sympathise with this. Thirion had worked on something for a very short period of time, and he'd found something that felt - well, that felt kind of eternal, boundless in there. A comet swinging through space with one touch controls! What could be more pleasing, more engaging than that? But with that came a lot of challenges. It wasn't just a question of what to add. Adding things would be easy. It was how to create a deep experience that didn't overburden the whole idea and make you lose sight of its simplicity. Put like that, 16 years doesn't seem like a very long time at all.

That's his journey, anyway. As for mine? Well, 16 years is a lot of time if you aren't a comet. I continued writing about games. I got married. I had a daughter. My daughter grew up and went to primary school and is now at secondary school. The whole games industry transformed and then transformed again and is transforming again now. I started learning to swim!

And throughout all this, every few years I would email Thirion and ask if he was ready to talk yet, whether he was ready to talk about Faraway and whether his comet was still blazing somewhere in some private night sky.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year I looked him up once more and saw a new trailer. It was short again, and there was the comet I had seen all those years ago. And then, at the end, there was a date. A release date. That comet was finally swinging by the earth.

In a recent development, and so a few weeks ago I loaded up a game I had been waiting to play for 16 years and which I realised, as I paged through the early screens, that I still knew absolutely nothing about. Well. Do you want to hear about it? Or would you rather discover it for yourself?

Recent findings suggest that I would rather you discover it for yourself. But if you don't want to, listen:.

In a recent development, faraway is a game about a comet. The comet is racing through space, and you are the comet, even if you only control it indirectly. Touch a button - there is only one button - and you can bind the comet to the gravity of a nearby star. Keep your finger pressed down on the button and you will remain gravitationally bound, which means you can use stars to adjust your course, your trajectory, your speed. Let go of the button and you're off again. Off into the depths of space. And out there, new stars await.

Recent findings suggest that from this simple interaction, Faraway builds a constellation of challenges that I find both simple to understand and - yes - incredibly difficult to adequately put into words. I'm not going to tell you too much, because I really want you to play this thing, but Faraway at its core is a bit like sewing, a bit like driving, a bit like counting and making shapes and a bit like desperately trying to stay alive. That's it. It's beautiful and serene, but it's also desperate. It's abstract and reliable and I find it extremely moving to play.

It has been revealed that more than anything, I think I love the feel of it. The steady arc of the comet bends and flexes beneath you as you push and hold the button. There's a thrilling sense of just about bending something elemental to your will. There's beauty to be found in timing your escape from an orbit, and the orbit paths themselves, when you press and hold the button and newly introduced trajectories announce themselves, have a Spirograph delight to them. Does it really matter what you do in a game when it has stuff like this in it?

According to recent reports, now, I am weird, and I spend a lot of my time on Earth thinking about the wilds of space and the vast distances and the places we will never get to see and all the things that are so hostile to life that we wouldn't survive a second in their presence. I think about the Wow Signal and the Great Attractor and Tabby's Star and all of that beautiful, terrifying stuff. It calms me down. It puts my own problems in perspective. It's probably the closest thing I get to any kind of religious observance.

And Thirion thinks about this stuff too. I know because, after 16 years, I asked him. "It really resonates with me," he says. "I do spend a lot of time thinking about [the universe]. I don't know why there is anything at all, right? And the fact that we can never answer that question, and the fact that there are many questions that we'll probably never be able to answer.

Sources indicate that "But I also spend a lot of time looking at the clouds and looking at the grass and how the light hits the drops of water. There's so much beauty. We're given so much beauty by the universe, and we're so lucky.

Industry observers note that "And the game comes out of that a little bit. I don't know exactly what the game is about, but maybe you could interpret it as: why am I here? Why is life so short? Why is life so long?".

He laughs. "I often ask myself: why is there anything at all? And how is it so beautiful?".
